OZNAL Capstone - LoL Esports Early-Game Prediction

Author

Martin Vančo, Adriana Gemeľová

Published

May 1, 2026

1 Introduction

League of Legends is the most-played and most-watched esport in the world. Predicting which team will win from the early state of the match is a long-standing question in esports analytics: by 15 minutes - well before half of a typical game has elapsed - gold, experience, and objective leads have already begun to compound. We use the 2025 season of professional play to test how reliably this 15-minute snapshot forecasts the eventual winner, and which features actually drive the prediction.

The analysis runs two scenarios on the same data:

  • Scenario 1 - Model Comparison. We train and tune five baseline classifiers (Logistic Regression, Random Forest, Naive Bayes, KNN, CART) on the early-game feature set, plus XGBoost as an additional model to mirror the gradient-boosted approach used in the published @15 literature. All six are compared on accuracy, AUC-ROC, precision, recall, and F1. The goal is to see whether any model can extract signal beyond the trivial “team with the gold lead at 15 min wins” baseline (~73% accuracy), and whether different model families agree on what matters.
  • Scenario 3 - Feature Selection. With 14 candidate features carrying residual redundancy, we apply forward stepwise selection (AIC), LASSO, and Elastic Net to find the minimal subset that retains predictive performance. This both improves interpretability and stress-tests which features are genuinely informative versus carrying duplicate signal.

1.1 Hypotheses

H1: “Early-game performance metrics and objective control can reliably predict match outcome in professional League of Legends.” We test whether gold, XP, and CS differentials at 10 and 15 minutes, combined with first objective captures (first blood, first dragon, first tower, void grubs), contain enough signal to classify wins and losses.

H2: “Bot lane (ADC) gold advantage is the most impactful role-specific early-game factor for predicting match outcome.” We test whether the bot lane player’s early-game differentials carry stronger predictive signal than those of other roles (top, jungle, mid, support).

1.2 Motivation

Both of us on this project are long-time League of Legends players and regular viewers of the professional scene. Watching pro matches, you very quickly develop a feel for when a game is “already over” - a significant gold lead at early game mostly means a quick and decisive game. We had been wondering for a while how much of that intuition is actually backed by data: how reliably do those early signals predict the eventual winner and which signals matter the most.

2 Dataset

We use the 2025 season export from Oracle’s Elixir [1], the standard public source for professional League of Legends match data. The raw file contains 120,636 rows across 165 columns, covering 10,053 unique matches played by 445 teams across 45 professional leagues (LPL, LCK, LEC, LFL, LAS, EM, …) on patches 15.01-15.24.

The row layout is 12 rows per game: one per player (5 per team) plus one aggregated team-level row per side (Blue and Red, 50/50). About 91.9% of rows are marked complete, meaning the early-game snapshots at 10/15/20/25 min are populated; the remaining 8.1% are missing these values.

Columns group into metadata (gameid, league, patch, side, position, …), draft (pick1-5, ban1-5), outcome (result, gamelength), combat (kills/deaths/assists, first blood), objectives (dragons, heralds, void grubs, towers, turret plates), economy (gold, CS), vision (wards, vision score), and the early-game timeline snapshots (goldatX, xpatX, csatX, golddiffatX, etc. for X in {10, 15, 20, 25}) which form the core of our feature set.

3 Game introduction

League of Legends (LoL) is a 5v5 team game. Two teams (Blue and Red side) try to destroy each other’s base. A single match is typically around 30 minutes but can last as long as 50 minutes. In this work, we focus on the early game stage (the first 15 minutes). Each team has five fixed roles - top, jungle (jng), mid, bot (ADC), and support (sup) - each playing a different lane or area of the map.

Three continuous resources accumulate throughout the match:

  • Gold - earned from minions, champion kills, and objectives, and spent on items that strengthen champions.
  • XP (experience) - levels champions up and unlocks abilities.
  • CS (creep score) - the number of minions a player has killed

The early game also has a set of one-off objective races, each won by exactly one team: first blood (the first champion kill of the match), first dragon, first herald, first tower (each granting a stacking buff, a tower-damaging summon, or a large gold bonus), turret plates (five plates on each outer tower, all paid out as gold before 14:00), and void grubs (a shared pit of up to 6 grubs that despawns at 13:45 on early-2025 patches and 14:45 mid-season).

4 Related work

Published work on early-game LoL match prediction at the 15-minute mark converges tightly, with reported accuracy clustering in the 76-78% band across model families and dataset types.

Study Year Dataset Model Acc. @15
Spaargaren, MSc thesis (Tilburg) [2] 2022 Oracle’s Elixir pro, 2021 Logistic Regression 77.99%
Spaargaren 2022 Oracle’s Elixir pro, 2021 Random Forest 77.26%
Spaargaren 2022 Oracle’s Elixir pro, 2021 Naïve Bayes 76.82%
Spaargaren 2022 Oracle’s Elixir pro, 2021 kNN (k=9) 74.83%
Lafrance & Grewal, Entertainment Computing [3] 2026 Riot API solo queue, Diamond XGBoost 76.9%
Junior & Campelo, arXiv 2309.02449 [4] 2023 Riot API solo queue Random Forest ~74%*

*Interpolated to 50% PET (≈ 15 min for a ~30-min median match) from Junior & Campelo’s PET-bucket accuracy curves.

Two takeaways. First, professional play is not materially easier to predict than solo queue at 15 minutes - Spaargaren’s pro-data LR sits within one percentage point of Lafrance & Grewal’s solo-queue XGBoost. Second, algorithm choice matters little: pro-data classifiers all land in the 77 ± 1% band, with solo-queue ~3 points lower. Across every study, gold differential is the strongest single feature, with first tower or first herald typically ranked next.

Tsang (2025, Medium) [5] adds a temporal signal: the coefficient of golddiffat15 has declined from above 1.0 in 2020-2023 to 0.83 in 2025, suggesting the 2025 season is harder to predict from a single gold-at-15 signal than any previous season. We additionally include two features absent from the @15-minute literature - turret plate differential and void grubs (introduced in 2025 season).

Finally, we note a framing gap: the trivial rule “team with a gold lead at 15 min wins” already delivers ~73% accuracy on professional data (we compute the exact figure on our own set in the EDA), so the 76-78% models above only beat this naive baseline by 3-5 points. We adopt this framing directly in our results.

5 Setup

.required_pkgs <- c(
    "tidyverse", "corrplot", "caret", "glmnet", "randomForest",
    "naivebayes", "rpart", "rpart.plot", "xgboost", "pROC",
    "gridExtra", "doParallel", "MASS"
)
.missing_pkgs <- setdiff(.required_pkgs, rownames(installed.packages()))
if (length(.missing_pkgs)) {
    install.packages(.missing_pkgs, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
}

library(tidyverse)
library(corrplot)
library(caret)
library(glmnet)
library(randomForest)
library(naivebayes)
library(rpart)
library(xgboost)
library(pROC)
library(gridExtra)
library(doParallel)

detected_cores <- parallel::detectCores(logical = TRUE)
if (is.na(detected_cores) || detected_cores < 2) {
    detected_cores <- 2
}

cl <- tryCatch(
    parallel::makePSOCKcluster(max(1, detected_cores - 1)),
    error = function(e) {
        message("Parallel backend unavailable; continuing sequentially: ", conditionMessage(e))
        NULL
    }
)

if (!is.null(cl)) {
    doParallel::registerDoParallel(cl)
} else {
    foreach::registerDoSEQ()
}

# select only complete data - with @10, 15, 20, 25 metrics
complete <- raw %>% filter(datacompleteness == "complete")

teams <- complete %>% filter(position == "team")
players <- complete %>% filter(position != "team")

cat(sprintf(
    "Total rows: %d\nFiltered to complete: %d (removed %d incomplete, %.1f%%)\nTeam rows: %d\nPlayer rows: %d\nTarget balance: %.1f%% win / %.1f%% loss",
    nrow(raw), nrow(complete),
    nrow(raw) - nrow(complete),
    (nrow(raw) - nrow(complete)) / nrow(raw) * 100,
    nrow(teams), nrow(players),
    mean(teams$result == 1) * 100, mean(teams$result == 0) * 100
))
Total rows: 120636
Filtered to complete: 110832 (removed 9804 incomplete, 8.1%)
Team rows: 18472
Player rows: 92360
Target balance: 50.0% win / 50.0% loss

5.2 Restructure: one row per game

The raw teams table stores two mirror rows per game, one per side. For EDA we pivot to one row per game with blue_* and red_* columns and a binary blue_win target, following the tidy data convention of one observation per row (Wickham, 2014, JSS 59(10)) [6].

After the pivot, the Blue and Red copies of each signed differential and each mutually-exclusive binary flag are pure mirrors: red_golddiffat15 = -blue_golddiffat15 and red_firstblood = 1 - blue_firstblood. We drop the red_* side of those columns, since the model gains nothing from a feature it can recover from the one next to it. Independent counts (kills, deaths, assists, turret plates) and the shared-pool grub count stay on both sides - neither side can be reconstructed from the other.

game_cols <- c(
    "result",
    "goldat10", "xpat10", "csat10",
    "goldat15", "xpat15", "csat15",
    "golddiffat10", "xpdiffat10", "csdiffat10",
    "golddiffat15", "xpdiffat15", "csdiffat15",
    "killsat10", "deathsat10", "assistsat10",
    "killsat15", "deathsat15", "assistsat15",
    "firstblood", "firstdragon", "firstherald", "firsttower",
    "void_grubs", "turretplates"
)

games_full <- teams %>%
    select(gameid, side, all_of(game_cols)) %>%
    mutate(side = tolower(side)) %>%
    pivot_wider(
        id_cols     = gameid,
        names_from  = side,
        values_from = all_of(game_cols),
        names_glue  = "{side}_{.value}"
    ) %>%
    mutate(blue_win = blue_result) %>%
    select(-blue_result, -red_result)

# Sanity: blue/red signed diffs must be exact negatives of each other,
# and mutually exclusive binary flags must satisfy red = 1 - blue whenever
# the objective fires.
stopifnot(all.equal(games_full$blue_golddiffat15, -games_full$red_golddiffat15))
stopifnot(all.equal(games_full$blue_xpdiffat15, -games_full$red_xpdiffat15))
stopifnot(all.equal(games_full$blue_csdiffat15, -games_full$red_csdiffat15))
stopifnot(all(games_full$blue_firstblood + games_full$redirstblood <= 1))
stopifnot(all(games_full$blue_firsttower + games_full$red_firsttower <= 1))

# Drop the strict-mirror columns identified above. We keep both sides for
# independent counts (kills/deaths/assists/turret plates) and for the
# shared-pool grub count, since those carry information beyond their pair.
redundant_mirrors <- c(
    "red_golddiffat10", "red_xpdiffat10", "red_csdiffat10",
    "red_golddiffat15", "red_xpdiffat15", "red_csdiffat15",
    "red_firstblood", "red_firstdragon", "red_firstherald", "red_firsttower"
)

games <- games_full %>% select(-all_of(redundant_mirrors))

cat(sprintf(
    "Games (one row per game): %d\nFeatures dropped as strict mirrors: %d\nFeatures retained: %d\nBlue win rate: %.2f%% (Red: %.2f%%)\n",
    nrow(games),
    length(redundant_mirrors),
    ncol(games) - 2, # excluding gameid and blue_win
    mean(games$blue_win) * 100,
    mean(1 - games$blue_win) * 100
))
Games (one row per game): 9236
Features dropped as strict mirrors: 10
Features retained: 38
Blue win rate: 53.28% (Red: 46.72%)
# Statistical test for side imbalance
side_test <- prop.test(sum(games$blue_win), nrow(games), p = 0.5)
cat(sprintf(
    "\nTwo-sided proportion test vs 50%%:\n  chi^2 = %.2f, df = 1, p = %.3g\n  95%% CI for Blue WR: [%.3f, %.3f]\n  -> Blue-side advantage is %s.\n",
    side_test$statistic, side_test$p.value,
    side_test$conf.int[1], side_test$conf.int[2],
    ifelse(side_test$p.value < 0.05, "statistically significant", "not statistically significant")
))

Two-sided proportion test vs 50%:
  chi^2 = 39.63, df = 1, p = 3.07e-10
  95% CI for Blue WR: [0.523, 0.543]
  -> Blue-side advantage is statistically significant.

Blue side wins slightly more than half of games. The imbalance is mild enough that no resampling is needed and accuracy remains valid alongside AUC-ROC.

6 Exploratory Data Analysis

Everything below uses the single-row-per-game games dataset. The aim is to see what signal is available and catch any issues before we start modelling.

6.1 Target distribution

games %>%
    mutate(blue_win = factor(blue_win, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("Red won", "Blue won"))) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = blue_win, fill = blue_win)) +
    geom_bar() +
    geom_text(stat = "count", aes(label = after_stat(count)), vjust = -0.5) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("Red won" = "#e74c3c", "Blue won" = "#3498db")) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = nrow(games) / 2, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40") +
    labs(
        title = "Target Variable Distribution (blue_win)",
        x = "Outcome", y = "Count"
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(legend.position = "none")

Blue wins slightly more than half of games (p < 0.001), but the imbalance is only roughly 3 percentage points above 50% - small enough to keep accuracy as a valid metric and skip resampling.

6.2 Descriptive statistics

We sort the early-game numerics by standard deviation. Features with much larger spread will dominate distance-based models like KNN unless they are scaled, which is why we centre and standardise later in the pipeline.

early_game_cols <- c(
    "blue_goldat10", "blue_xpat10", "blue_csat10",
    "blue_golddiffat10", "blue_xpdiffat10", "blue_csdiffat10",
    "blue_killsat10", "blue_deathsat10", "blue_assistsat10",
    "blue_goldat15", "blue_xpat15", "blue_csat15",
    "blue_golddiffat15", "blue_xpdiffat15", "blue_csdiffat15",
    "blue_killsat15", "blue_deathsat15", "blue_assistsat15",
    "blue_firstblood", "blue_firstdragon", "blue_firstherald", "blue_firsttower",
    "blue_void_grubs", "red_void_grubs",
    "blue_turretplates", "red_turretplates",
    "blue_win"
)

games %>%
    select(all_of(setdiff(early_game_cols, "blue_win"))) %>%
    pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "feature", values_to = "value") %>%
    drop_na() %>%
    group_by(feature) %>%
    summarise(
        n = n(),
        mean = mean(value),
        sd = sd(value),
        min = min(value),
        q25 = quantile(value, 0.25),
        median = median(value),
        q75 = quantile(value, 0.75),
        max = max(value),
        .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    mutate(across(c(mean, sd, min, q25, median, q75, max), ~ round(.x, 2))) %>%
    arrange(desc(sd)) %>%
    print(n = Inf)

Gold and XP have the widest spread, with standard deviations in the thousands; @15 totals cluster around 25k gold and 30k XP. CS columns are an order of magnitude smaller, kill/death/assist counts smaller still, and the 0/1 objectives sit at the bottom with sd around 0.5. The differentials (blue_minus_red) average close to zero (243 gold and 49 XP at 15), which is what we would expect across balanced matches - the small positive offset reflects the Blue-side advantage.

6.3 Early-game feature correlations with blue_win

We correlate each early-game numeric feature (Blue’s perspective) with the target.

cor_data <- games %>%
    select(all_of(early_game_cols)) %>%
    drop_na()

cor_matrix <- cor(cor_data)

corrplot(cor_matrix,
    method = "color", type = "lower",
    tl.cex = 0.7, tl.col = "black",
    col = colorRampPalette(c("#e74c3c", "white", "#2ecc71"))(200),
    col.lim = c(-1, 1),
    title = "Correlation Matrix - Early-Game Features (Blue's perspective)",
    mar = c(0, 0, 2, 0)
)
result_cors <- cor_data %>%
    select(-blue_win) %>%
    summarise(across(everything(), ~ cor(.x, cor_data$blue_win))) %>%
    pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "feature", values_to = "correlation") %>%
    arrange(desc(abs(correlation)))

ggplot(result_cors, aes(
    x    = reorder(feature, abs(correlation)),
    y    = correlation,
    fill = correlation > 0
)) +
    geom_col() +
    coord_flip(ylim = c(-1, 1)) +
    scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(-1, 1, 0.25)) +
    scale_fill_manual(
        values = c("TRUE" = "#2ecc71", "FALSE" = "#e74c3c"),
        labels = c("Negative", "Positive")
    ) +
    labs(
        title = "Feature Correlation with blue_win",
        x = NULL, y = "Pearson Correlation", fill = "Direction"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()
cat(sprintf(
    "Strongest positive: %s (%.3f)\nStrongest negative: %s (%.3f)",
    result_cors$feature[which.max(result_cors$correlation)],
    max(result_cors$correlation),
    result_cors$feature[which.min(result_cors$correlation)],
    min(result_cors$correlation)
))
Strongest positive: blue_golddiffat15 (0.520)
Strongest negative: red_turretplates (-0.297)

Differentials (blue_golddiffat15, blue_xpdiffat15, blue_csdiffat15) dominate - what matters is the gap, not the absolute totals. Among objectives, blue_firsttower and blue_firstherald stand out, while blue_firstblood and blue_firstdragon are weaker. The matrix also shows two multicollinearity patterns: a raw stat against its own differential (blue_goldat15 vs blue_golddiffat15), and Blue/Red shared-pool pairs - blue_void_grubs and red_void_grubs are negatively correlated because the 6-grub pit is shared between the two teams. Both patterns motivate the LASSO and Elastic Net regularization used in Scenario 3.

6.4 Per-outcome means

    select(all_of(early_game_cols)) %>%
    drop_na() %>%
    mutate(outcome = if_else(blue_win == 1, "blue_win", "red_win")) %>%
    select(-blue_win) %>%
    pivot_longer(-outcome, names_to = "feature", values_to = "value") %>%
    group_by(feature, outcome) %>%
    summarise(mean = mean(value), .groups = "drop") %>%
    pivot_wider(names_from = outcome, values_from = mean) %>%
    mutate(diff = blue_win - red_win) %>%
    arrange(desc(abs(diff))) %>%
    mutate(across(c(blue_win, red_win, diff), ~ round(.x, 3))) %>%
    print(n = Inf)

Gold and XP differentials at 15 minutes produce the largest gaps. When Blue wins, it leads by ~1500 gold and ~940 XP at 15 min; when it loses, it trails by roughly the same amount. Among the 0/1 features, blue_firsttower jumps from 0.33 in losses to 0.73 in wins and blue_firstherald from 0.44 to 0.75, while first blood and first dragon shift the means by less than 0.17. blue_deathsat15 is the only count where the win-mean is lower than the loss-mean (3.6 vs 5.2), and red_void_grubs is negatively associated with blue_win because grubs taken by the enemy team hurt Blue.

6.5 Gold differential distribution

Gold differential at 15 minutes is the single strongest early-game predictor. The plots below show how cleanly it separates wins from losses and whether a simple threshold already captures most of the signal.

games %>%
    filter(!is.na(blue_golddiffat15)) %>%
    mutate(blue_win = factor(blue_win, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("Red won", "Blue won"))) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = blue_golddiffat15, fill = blue_win)) +
    geom_density(alpha = 0.5) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("Red won" = "#e74c3c", "Blue won" = "#3498db")) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40") +
    labs(
        title = "Gold Differential at 15 Minutes - Blue's Perspective",
        x = "blue_golddiffat15", y = "Density", fill = "Outcome"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()
games %>%
    filter(!is.na(blue_golddiffat10), !is.na(blue_golddiffat15)) %>%
    mutate(blue_win = factor(blue_win, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("Red won", "Blue won"))) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = blue_golddiffat10, y = blue_golddiffat15, color = blue_win)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.15, size = 0.8) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c("Red won" = "#e74c3c", "Blue won" = "#3498db")) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40") +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40") +
    labs(
        title = "Blue Gold Diff @10 vs @15 - Do Leads Grow?",
        x = "blue_golddiffat10", y = "blue_golddiffat15", color = "Outcome"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()

We score the naive rule “Blue ahead in gold @15 -> Blue wins” directly on games. The result defines the baseline any trained model has to beat.

gold_baseline_df <- games %>%
    filter(!is.na(blue_golddiffat15)) %>%
    transmute(
        pred_blue_win = blue_golddiffat15 > 0,
        actual        = blue_win == 1
    )

gold_baseline_acc <- mean(gold_baseline_df$pred_blue_win == gold_baseline_df$actual)
gold_baseline_n <- nrow(gold_baseline_df)
gold_baseline_ties <- sum(games$blue_golddiffat15 == 0, na.rm = TRUE)
blue_base_rate <- mean(games$blue_win)

cat(sprintf(
    "Naive rule 'Blue ahead in gold @15 -> Blue wins':\n  N = %d games (%d games tied at exactly 0 gold diff)\n  Accuracy: %.2f%%\n  Always-predict-Blue baseline: %.2f%%\n  Rule beats always-Blue by: %.2f pp",
    gold_baseline_n, gold_baseline_ties,
    gold_baseline_acc * 100,
    blue_base_rate * 100,
    (gold_baseline_acc - blue_base_rate) * 100
))
Naive rule 'Blue ahead in gold @15 -> Blue wins':
  N = 9236 games (1 games tied at exactly 0 gold diff)
  Accuracy: 72.88%
  Always-predict-Blue baseline: 53.28%
  Rule beats always-Blue by: 19.60 pp

The two densities are clearly separated. The naive rule hits 72.9% accuracy - well above the 50% coin-flip and the 53.3% always-Blue baseline - and any model has to beat it to be worth keeping. The wide overlap around zero leaves room for non-linear models to find signal beyond gold alone.

6.6 First objective win rates

The four “first” objectives (first blood, first dragon, first herald, first tower) all happen in the first ~14 minutes; exactly one team secures each. For every objective we compute the securer’s win rate and a chi-square test of independence against outcome.

obj_cols <- c("firstblood", "firstdragon", "firstherald", "firsttower")

obj_winrates <- map_dfr(obj_cols, function(obj) {
    blue_col <- paste0("blue_", obj)
    df <- games %>%
        select(all_of(c(blue_col, "blue_win"))) %>%
        drop_na()

    n_blue <- sum(df[[blue_col]] == 1)
    n_red <- sum(df[[blue_col]] == 0)
    blue_wr <- mean(df$blue_win[df[[blue_col]] == 1]) * 100
    red_wr <- mean(df$blue_win[df[[blue_col]] == 0]) * 100 # P(Blue wins | Red secured)

    chi <- chisq.test(table(df[[blue_col]], df$blue_win))

    tibble(
        objective     = str_replace(obj, "first", "First ") %>% str_to_title(),
        secured_by    = c("Blue secured", "Red secured"),
        win_rate_blue = c(blue_wr, red_wr),
        n             = c(n_blue, n_red),
        chi2          = chi$statistic,
        p_value       = chi$p.value
    )
})

ggplot(
    obj_winrates,
    aes(x = reorder(objective, win_rate_blue), y = win_rate_blue, fill = secured_by)
) +
    geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.7), width = 0.6) +
    geom_text(
        aes(label = sprintf("%.1f%% (n=%d)", win_rate_blue, n)),
        position = position_dodge(width = 0.7),
        hjust = -0.05, size = 3
    ) +
    coord_flip() +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("Blue secured" = "#3498db", "Red secured" = "#e74c3c")) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 100)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 50, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40") +
    labs(
        title = "P(Blue wins) by Who Secured the First Objective",
        x = NULL, y = "Blue Win Rate (%)", fill = NULL
    ) +
    theme_minimal()
obj_winrates %>%
    distinct(objective, chi2, p_value) %>%
    mutate(
        chi2    = round(chi2, 1),
        p_value = formatC(p_value, format = "e", digits = 2)
    ) %>%
    print()
# A tibble: 4 × 3
  objective     chi2 p_value  
  <chr>        <dbl> <chr>    
1 First Blood   219. 1.45e-49 
2 First Dragon  275. 1.11e-61 
3 First Herald  960. 9.29e-211
4 First Tower  1467. 5.00e-321

When Blue secures first tower or first herald, Blue’s win rate jumps well above 50%, and drops by a similar amount when Red gets them; first blood and first dragon move it much less. Every chi-square rejects independence at p ≪ 0.001, so the direction is clear in all four cases - only the size of the effect differs. All four are worth keeping as features; we expect tower and herald to end up with the largest model coefficients in the LR fit and the highest importance scores in the tree-based models.

6.7 Void grubs

Void grubs are a 2024+ objective: they spawn at 5:00 and despawn at 13:45 on early-2025 patches (moved to 14:45 mid-season), so they are purely early-game. The pit holds up to 6 grubs split between the teams.

games %>%
    filter(!is.na(blue_void_grubs)) %>%
    group_by(blue_void_grubs) %>%
    summarise(
        win_rate = mean(blue_win) * 100,
        n        = n(),
        .groups  = "drop"
    ) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = factor(blue_void_grubs), y = win_rate, fill = win_rate)) +
    geom_col() +
    geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f%%\nn=%d", win_rate, n)),
        vjust = -0.3, size = 3
    ) +
    scale_fill_gradient(low = "#e74c3c", high = "#3498db") +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 100)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 50, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40") +
    labs(
        title = "Blue Win Rate by Number of Void Grubs Blue Secured",
        x = "blue_void_grubs", y = "P(Blue wins) (%)"
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(legend.position = "none")

The relationship is essentially monotonic: 0 grubs sits well below 50% win rate, 6 grubs climbs to ~70%. That justifies the grub differential built later. Wobbles at intermediate counts reflect low sample sizes - split outcomes are rare because grub fights usually end with one side taking the remaining set.

6.8 Side advantage

Blue gets first pick in the draft and has slight map asymmetries. We report the share of Blue wins with a 95% CI and a chi-square test against the 50% null.

n_games <- nrow(games)
n_blue <- sum(games$blue_win)
side_pt <- prop.test(n_blue, n_games, p = 0.5)
blue_wr <- n_blue / n_games * 100
ci_low <- side_pt$conf.int[1] * 100
ci_high <- side_pt$conf.int[2] * 100

tibble(
    label    = "Blue side",
    win_rate = blue_wr,
    ci_low   = ci_low,
    ci_high  = ci_high
) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = label, y = win_rate)) +
    geom_col(width = 0.4, fill = "#3498db") +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = ci_low, ymax = ci_high), width = 0.15, color = "gray20") +
    geom_text(
        aes(label = sprintf(
            "%.2f%%  [%.2f, %.2f]\nn=%d  ·  chi^2=%.1f, p=%.2g",
            win_rate, ci_low, ci_high, n_games,
            side_pt$statistic, side_pt$p.value
        )),
        vjust = -0.6, size = 3.5
    ) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 50, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40") +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 70)) +
    labs(
        title = "Blue-Side Advantage",
        x = NULL, y = "P(Blue wins) (%)"
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(legend.position = "none")

Blue wins ~53% of games - a steady ~3 pp edge that is small but consistent across patches, driven mainly by Blue picking first in champion select (which lets it lock the strongest contested champion of the patch before Red can) and by minor map and camera asymmetries that make objectives slightly easier to track and contest from Blue’s side.

6.9 Role-specific gold differentials (H2 preview)

As a first look at H2, we correlate each Blue-side player’s gold differential at 15 min with blue_win, broken out by role.

role_diffs_blue <- players %>%
    filter(
        position %in% c("top", "jng", "mid", "bot", "sup"),
        side == "Blue",
        !is.na(golddiffat15)
    ) %>%
    select(gameid, position, golddiffat15)

role_cors <- role_diffs_blue %>%
    inner_join(games %>% select(gameid, blue_win), by = "gameid") %>%
    group_by(position) %>%
    summarise(
        correlation     = cor(golddiffat15, blue_win),
        mean_diff_win   = mean(golddiffat15[blue_win == 1]),
        mean_diff_loss  = mean(golddiffat15[blue_win == 0]),
        .groups         = "drop"
    ) %>%
    mutate(position = toupper(position))

ggplot(role_cors, aes(
    x = reorder(position, correlation),
    y = correlation, fill = correlation
)) +
    geom_col() +
    geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("r = %.3f", correlation)),
        hjust = -0.1, size = 3.5
    ) +
    coord_flip() +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.42)) +
    scale_fill_gradient(low = "#f39c12", high = "#2ecc71") +
    labs(
        title = "Correlation: Role Gold Diff @15 (Blue side) vs blue_win",
        x = NULL, y = "Pearson Correlation with blue_win"
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(legend.position = "none")
role_diffs_blue %>%
    inner_join(games %>% select(gameid, blue_win), by = "gameid") %>%
    mutate(
        blue_win = factor(blue_win, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("Red won", "Blue won")),
        position = toupper(position)
    ) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = position, y = golddiffat15, fill = blue_win)) +
    geom_boxplot(outlier.alpha = 0.1) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("Red won" = "#e74c3c", "Blue won" = "#3498db")) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40") +
    labs(
        title = "Blue-Side Player Gold Differential @15 by Role and Outcome",
        x = "Role", y = "Gold Diff @15 min", fill = "Outcome"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()

Bot lane (ADC) has the highest correlation with blue_win - early evidence for H2. Inter-role gaps are small, though, so the full H2 test decides whether the lead is real or noise. The boxplot shows clear win/loss separation for every role; bot lane simply has the widest gap.

6.10 Feature distributions and scaling check

KNN and Logistic Regression are scale-sensitive; tree-based models and Naive Bayes are not. We check per-feature ranges below to decide whether standardisation is needed.

scale_check <- games %>%
    select(
        blue_goldat15, blue_xpat15, blue_csat15, blue_killsat15,
        blue_golddiffat15, blue_xpdiffat15, blue_csdiffat15,
        blue_void_grubs
    ) %>%
    drop_na() %>%
    pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "feature", values_to = "value")

ggplot(scale_check, aes(x = value)) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "#3498db", alpha = 0.7) +
    facet_wrap(~feature, scales = "free", ncol = 4) +
    labs(
        title = "Feature Distributions - Scale Check (Blue's perspective)",
        x = "Value", y = "Count"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()

Scales differ wildly: blue_goldat15 runs from ~20,000 to ~36,000, blue_void_grubs lives on 0-6, and blue_killsat15 on 0-24. Without standardisation, KNN distances would be swamped by gold (1000x larger than the rest) and effectively ignore kills and grubs, and LR coefficients would not be comparable across features. We z-score standardise before fitting KNN and Logistic Regression; tree-based models (RF, CART) and Naive Bayes do not need it.

6.11 EDA Summary

  1. Target is mildly imbalanced (~53/47 in Blue’s favour). Significant but small - accuracy is still a valid metric and no resampling is needed.
  2. Gold diff @15 is the strongest single predictor. The naive “gold-leader wins” rule already hits ~73% accuracy - the baseline to beat.
  3. Residual multicollinearity remains between raw stats and their differentials and between Blue/Red paired counts. Linear models need regularisation even after dropping strict mirrors.
  4. First tower and first herald swing Blue’s win rate sharply (chi-square p ≪ 0.001); they are the highest-impact binary objectives.
  5. First blood and first dragon are statistically significant but carry weaker signal than tower or herald - both shift Blue’s WR by ~10-15 pp when Blue secures, but only ~3-5 pp when Red does. The asymmetry comes from the herald-dragon trade pattern: Blue takes herald in 61% of games while Red free-takes dragon in 62%, so games where Red secured first dragon are biased toward games where Blue was already ahead.
  6. Void grubs show a near-monotonic gradient in Blue’s win rate from 0 to 6 grubs, which justifies engineering a grub differential.
  7. Blue-side advantage is significant (~53% win rate, 95% CI excludes 50%) and absorbed into the base rate of blue_win.
  8. Feature scales differ by ~1000x, so KNN and Logistic Regression need standardisation.
  9. Bot lane has the highest role-specific correlation with blue_win, supporting the H2 analysis.
  10. Leads tend to grow between @10 and @15.
  11. Turret plate differential is a strong feature that is purely early-game, since plates fall by 14:00. It rarely appears in the published @15 literature.
  12. Total dragon/herald counts are full-game statistics - using them would leak the outcome and they must not enter the feature set.

7 Feature Engineering

The correlation analysis indicates that gaps between teams carry the signal, so we retain signed differentials throughout. To control multicollinearity, we keep one element of each redundant triple (goldat15, opp_goldat15, golddiffat15) - the differential - and drop the other two. The raw @10 snapshots are likewise omitted: any signal they carry beyond the @15 snapshot is marginal, and combining them with the @15 differentials inflates VIF without raising held-out AUC. We supplement this core with two features that rarely appear in the published @15 literature: a turret plate differential (plates fall by 14:00, so the metric is purely early-game; r = 0.409 with blue_win) and a rolling team win rate differential, computed from prior games only.

We also evaluated several higher-order constructs - per-window momentum (diff@15 - diff@10 for gold, XP, and CS) and per-team kill-pressure counts in the 10–15 minute window. Each was a linear combination of features already present in the matrix and, in pilot fits, added severe multicollinearity without contributing any independent predictive signal, so all of them were dropped before the modelling pipeline. We retained two non-linear ratio features that do not introduce the same redundancy: gold_efficiency_15 = goldat15 / csat15 (gold-per-CS, a draft and macro proxy) and kda_15 = (kills + assists) / max(deaths, 1) (combat efficiency); both remain weakly correlated with the rest of the matrix.

7.1 Rolling team win rate

For each team, we compute a rolling win rate over all of its prior games, ordered by date, with first-appearance teams defaulted to 0.5. The per-side values are pivoted into one Blue and one Red column per game, and winrate_diff = blue - red captures pre-game asymmetry without leaking information from the current result

team_wr <- teams %>%
    arrange(date, gameid) %>%
    group_by(teamid) %>%
    mutate(
        games_before = row_number() - 1,
        wins_before  = cumsum(result) - result,
        team_winrate = ifelse(games_before > 0, wins_before / games_before, 0.5)
    ) %>%
    ungroup() %>%
    mutate(side = tolower(side)) %>%
    select(gameid, side, team_winrate, games_before) %>%
    pivot_wider(
        id_cols     = gameid,
        names_from  = side,
        values_from = c(team_winrate, games_before),
        names_glue  = "{side}_{.value}"
    )

games_wr <- games %>%
    left_join(team_wr, by = "gameid") %>%
    mutate(winrate_diff = blue_team_winrate - red_team_winrate)

cat(sprintf(
    "Median prior games: %.0f Blue / %.0f Red\nFirst-appearance teams (defaulted to 0.5): %d Blue, %d Red\nwinrate_diff correlation with blue_win: %.3f",
    median(games_wr$blue_games_before),
    median(games_wr$red_games_before),
    sum(games_wr$blue_games_before == 0),
    sum(games_wr$red_games_before == 0),
    cor(games_wr$winrate_diff, games_wr$blue_win, use = "complete.obs")
))
Median prior games: 31 Blue / 30 Red
First-appearance teams (defaulted to 0.5): 192 Blue, 190 Red
winrate_diff correlation with blue_win: 0.266

7.2 Select and engineer features

Every feature below is expressed from the Blue perspective: signed differentials in which a positive value indicates that Blue is ahead, together with four binary flags marking whether Blue secured each first objective. Since the perspective is fixed, the blue_ prefix is implicit throughout the modelling stage and is omitted from column names. Each row represents one full match, so the structural Blue-side advantage is absorbed into the base rate of blue_win and serves as the intercept of the model.

games_model <- games_wr %>%
    transmute(
        gameid,
        blue_win,

        # Snapshot diffs at 15 (primary signal, Blue's perspective)
        golddiffat15 = blue_golddiffat15,
        xpdiffat15 = blue_xpdiffat15,
        csdiffat15 = blue_csdiffat15,

        # Combat diffs at 15 (death_diff omitted: near-perfect mirror of -kill_diff, see VIF)
        kill_diff_15 = blue_killsat15 - red_killsat15,
        assist_diff_15 = blue_assistsat15 - red_assistsat15,

        # Non-linear early-game ratios (low VIF against the diff core)
        gold_efficiency_15 = blue_goldat15 / pmax(blue_csat15, 1),
        kda_15 = (blue_killsat15 + blue_assistsat15) / pmax(blue_deathsat15, 1),

        # Objective differentials
        plate_diff = blue_turretplates - red_turretplates,
        grub_diff = blue_void_grubs - red_void_grubs,

        # Pre-game strength
        winrate_diff,

        # First-objective flags (1 if Blue secured)
        firstblood = blue_firstblood,
        firstdragon = blue_firstdragon,
        firstherald = blue_firstherald,
        firsttower = blue_firsttower
    ) %>%
    drop_na()

cat(sprintf(
    "Final feature set: %d features (excluding gameid and blue_win)\nFeatures: %s",
    ncol(games_model) - 2,
    paste(setdiff(names(games_model), c("gameid", "blue_win")), collapse = ", ")
))
Final feature set: 14 features (excluding gameid and blue_win)
Features: golddiffat15, xpdiffat15, csdiffat15, kill_diff_15, assist_diff_15, gold_efficiency_15, kda_15, plate_diff, grub_diff, winrate_diff, firstblood, firstdragon, firstherald, firsttower

7.3 H2: Role-specific differentials

For H2 we add per-role early-game differentials. The signed golddiffat15 of each Blue-side player is, by construction, blue_player_gold - red_lane_opponent_gold; retaining only the Blue rows and pivoting wide therefore yields a Blue-perspective signed differential per role and per metric (e.g., bot_golddiffat15, mid_xpdiffat10). The resulting table is inner-joined back to games_model.

role_diffs <- players %>%
    filter(
        position %in% c("top", "jng", "mid", "bot", "sup"),
        side == "Blue"
    ) %>%
    select(
        gameid, position,
        golddiffat10, golddiffat15,
        xpdiffat10, xpdiffat15,
        csdiffat10, csdiffat15
    ) %>%
    drop_na() %>%
    pivot_wider(
        id_cols = gameid,
        names_from = position,
        values_from = c(
            golddiffat10, golddiffat15,
            xpdiffat10, xpdiffat15,
            csdiffat10, csdiffat15
        ),
        names_glue = "{position}_{.value}"
    )

games_h2 <- games_model %>%
    inner_join(role_diffs, by = "gameid") %>%
    drop_na()

cat(sprintf(
    "Role features added: %d\nH2 rows after join + drop_na: %d (removed %d from H1 set, %.1f%%)\nH2 total features: %d",
    ncol(role_diffs) - 1,
    nrow(games_h2),
    nrow(games_model) - nrow(games_h2),
    (nrow(games_model) - nrow(games_h2)) / nrow(games_model) * 100,
    ncol(games_h2) - 2
))
Role features added: 30
H2 rows after join + drop_na: 9236 (removed 0 from H1 set, 0.0%)
H2 total features: 44

8 Train/Test Split

Each row in games_model represents one full match, so a plain 80/20 row split is sufficient. We sample game IDs once with set.seed(42) and reuse the same partition for H2, ensuring that both hypotheses are evaluated on the same held-out games.

set.seed(42)

train_ids <- sample(games_model$gameid, size = floor(0.8 * nrow(games_model)))

train_h1 <- games_model %>%
    filter(gameid %in% train_ids) %>%
    select(-gameid)
test_h1 <- games_model %>%
    filter(!gameid %in% train_ids) %>%
    select(-gameid)

train_h2 <- games_h2 %>%
    filter(gameid %in% train_ids) %>%
    select(-gameid)
test_h2 <- games_h2 %>%
    filter(!gameid %in% train_ids) %>%
    select(-gameid)

cat(sprintf(
    "Games: %d train, %d test\nH1 - Train: %d rows, Test: %d rows\nH2 - Train: %d rows, Test: %d rows",
    length(train_ids), nrow(games_model) - length(train_ids),
    nrow(train_h1), nrow(test_h1), nrow(train_h2), nrow(test_h2)
))
Games: 7388 train, 1848 test
H1 - Train: 7388 rows, Test: 1848 rows
H2 - Train: 7388 rows, Test: 1848 rows

9 Scenario 1: Model Comparison

Six classifiers on the same H1 feature set, judged on accuracy, AUC-ROC, precision, recall, and F1. Hyperparameters are tuned with shared 5-fold CV (metric = "ROC"); the test set is held out for the final report.

Category Model Role in the comparison
Statistical/ML Logistic Regression Interpretable linear baseline; standardised coefficients
Statistical/ML Random Forest Non-linear ensemble; agreement check on what matters
Statistical/ML Naive Bayes Bayes-rule baseline assuming feature independence
Partitioning KNN Distance-based; sensitive to scale and correlated features
Partitioning Decision Tree (CART) Single-tree analogue of RF for the consensus comparison
Statistical/ML XGBoost Gradient-boosted trees; benchmark used in modern LoL @15 prediction papers

The bar to beat is the EDA baseline: 72.9 % from “Blue ahead in gold @15 wins”. Published @15 LoL studies report 73-78 %, so a 75 %-band result is consistent with the literature.

9.1 Preprocessing

KNN and Logistic Regression need standardised inputs. We fit the scaler on the training set and apply the same transformation to the test set. Tree-based models (RF, CART, XGBoost) and Naive Bayes do not need scaling, but reusing the scaled matrix is harmless.

X_train <- train_h1 %>% select(-blue_win)
y_train <- train_h1$blue_win
X_test <- test_h1 %>% select(-blue_win)
y_test <- test_h1$blue_win

preproc <- preProcess(X_train, method = c("center", "scale"))
X_train_scaled <- predict(preproc, X_train)
X_test_scaled <- predict(preproc, X_test)

cat(sprintf(
    "Training features: %d   Training rows: %d   Test rows: %d\n",
    ncol(X_train), nrow(X_train), nrow(X_test)
))
Training features: 14   Training rows: 7388   Test rows: 1848

9.2 Multicollinearity check (VIF)

VIF (Variance Inflation Factor) tells us how much each feature overlaps with the rest of the matrix. A high VIF means the feature can be largely reproduced from the others; values above 10 are conventionally treated as a sign of severe collinearity. We compute it on the training set only - VIF is a fit-time diagnostic and must not be informed by held-out data.

vif_df <- tibble(
    feature = names(X_train_scaled),
    VIF     = diag(solve(cor(X_train_scaled)))
) %>% arrange(desc(VIF))

knitr::kable(vif_df,
    digits = 2,
    caption = "VIF on H1 training features (diagnostic only - no features dropped in S1)."
)
VIF on H1 training features (diagnostic only - no features dropped in S1).
feature VIF
golddiffat15 22.90
kill_diff_15 12.57
assist_diff_15 5.24
xpdiffat15 5.17
csdiffat15 4.58
plate_diff 3.54
kda_15 2.37
firsttower 1.63
grub_diff 1.32
firstherald 1.24
gold_efficiency_15 1.24
firstblood 1.22
winrate_diff 1.12
firstdragon 1.10

Two features exceed the threshold: golddiffat15 (≈ 23) and kill_diff_15 (≈ 13). Gold and kills are tightly coupled in League - every kill pays out gold and pushes the lane further ahead - so most of what kill_diff_15 carries is already in golddiffat15. xpdiffat15, csdiffat15, and assist_diff_15 sit in the 4–5 range, reflecting the same lane-economy signal at a weaker level. The binary objective flags, winrate_diff, and the two ratio features (gold_efficiency_15, kda_15) all stay below VIF 4 and are effectively independent.

Three of our six models are affected by this. Logistic Regression coefficients become unstable when predictors overlap, Naive Bayes assumes feature independence outright, and KNN distances double-count correlated dimensions. Random Forest, CART, and XGBoost split one feature at a time and are unaffected.

ImportantWhy we do not drop high-VIF features here

The standard rule of thumb is to drop features with VIF > 10. The two features above the threshold here are golddiffat15 - the strongest single predictor in the problem - and kill_diff_15, its closest economic partner. Their VIF is high because the other features overlap with them, not because they themselves carry no signal: VIF measures redundancy, not predictive value. We keep every surviving feature in S1, treat VIF as a diagnostic only, and let the regularised methods in S3 (LASSO and Elastic Net) handle the residual redundancy.

9.3 CV setup

Shared trainControl so every model is tuned on the same folds.

ctrl <- trainControl(
    method = "cv",
    number = 5,
    classProbs = TRUE,
    summaryFunction = twoClassSummary,
    savePredictions = "final",
    verboseIter = FALSE
)

y_train_fct <- factor(y_train, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("Loss", "Win"))
y_test_fct <- factor(y_test, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("Loss", "Win"))

9.4 Logistic Regression

Linear baseline trained on the standardised feature matrix so coefficients are directly comparable. With Win as the last factor level, glm models log-odds of Win - a positive coefficient indicates the feature pushes towards Blue winning, a negative one pushes against.

t0 <- Sys.time()

lr_model <- train(
    x = X_train_scaled,
    y = y_train_fct,
    method = "glm",
    family = "binomial",
    trControl = ctrl,
    metric = "ROC"
)

lr_pred <- predict(lr_model, X_test_scaled)
lr_prob <- predict(lr_model, X_test_scaled, type = "prob")
lr_cm <- confusionMatrix(lr_pred, y_test_fct, positive = "Win")

cat(sprintf(
    "\nLogistic Regression Results (trained in %.1fs):\nAccuracy: %.1f%%\nSensitivity (Win recall): %.1f%%\nSpecificity (Loss recall): %.1f%%\nCV AUC-ROC: %.3f",
    as.numeric(Sys.time() - t0, units = "secs"),
    lr_cm$overall["Accuracy"] * 100,
    lr_cm$byClass["Sensitivity"] * 100,
    lr_cm$byClass["Specificity"] * 100,
    max(lr_model$results$ROC)
))

Logistic Regression Results (trained in 5.5s):
Accuracy: 75.5%
Sensitivity (Win recall): 79.1%
Specificity (Loss recall): 71.2%
CV AUC-ROC: 0.843
lr_coefs <- coef(lr_model$finalModel) %>%
    as.data.frame() %>%
    rownames_to_column("feature") %>%
    rename(coefficient = 2) %>%
    filter(feature != "(Intercept)") %>%
    arrange(desc(abs(coefficient)))

ggplot(
    lr_coefs,
    aes(
        x = reorder(feature, abs(coefficient)),
        y = coefficient,
        fill = coefficient > 0
    )
) +
    geom_col() +
    coord_flip() +
    scale_fill_manual(
        values = c("TRUE" = "#2ecc71", "FALSE" = "#e74c3c"),
        breaks = c("TRUE", "FALSE"),
        labels = c("Positive", "Negative")
    ) +
    labs(
        title = "Logistic Regression - Standardised coefficients",
        x = NULL, y = "Coefficient", fill = "Direction"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()

All non-trivial coefficients are positive: resource diffs at @15 (golddiffat15, xpdiffat15, csdiffat15), kill_diff_15, winrate_diff, and the first-objective flags all push toward Blue winning, exactly as the EDA predicted. firstblood is the only feature with a negative coefficient and its magnitude is essentially zero - consistent with the EDA showing it as the weakest of the four objective flags. There are no sign flips on the high-VIF pair, which is what we’d expect: the residual collinearity is moderate enough that LR can still attribute coefficients to roughly the right direction, even if SEs on golddiffat15 and kill_diff_15 are mildly inflated. S3’s regularised methods will tighten this further by zeroing out the marginal contributors.

9.5 Random Forest

Non-linear ensemble; immune to the residual multicollinearity in the LR coefficient table. We tune mtry over {3, 5, 7, 10, 14} with 500 trees fixed.

t0 <- Sys.time()

rf_model <- train(
    x = X_train,
    y = y_train_fct,
    method = "rf",
    trControl = ctrl,
    metric = "ROC",
    tuneGrid = expand.grid(mtry = c(3, 5, 7, 10, 14)),
    ntree = 500
)

rf_pred <- predict(rf_model, X_test)
rf_prob <- predict(rf_model, X_test, type = "prob")
rf_cm <- confusionMatrix(rf_pred, y_test_fct, positive = "Win")

cat(sprintf(
    "\nRandom Forest Results (trained in %.1fs):\nAccuracy: %.1f%%\nSensitivity: %.1f%%\nSpecificity: %.1f%%\nBest mtry: %d\nCV AUC-ROC: %.3f",
    as.numeric(Sys.time() - t0, units = "secs"),
    rf_cm$overall["Accuracy"] * 100,
    rf_cm$byClass["Sensitivity"] * 100,
    rf_cm$byClass["Specificity"] * 100,
    rf_model$bestTune$mtry,
    max(rf_model$results$ROC)
))

ggplot(
    rf_imp,
    aes(x = reorder(feature, Overall), y = Overall)
) +
    geom_col(fill = "#27ae60") +
    coord_flip() +
    labs(
        title = "Random Forest - Feature importances",
        x = NULL, y = "Importance"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()

9.6 Naive Bayes

The independence assumption is directly violated by the VIF result above; we still fit it to see how much accuracy that costs. We tune usekernel (Gaussian vs KDE) and the KDE bandwidth multiplier adjust.

t0 <- Sys.time()

nb_grid <- expand.grid(
    usekernel = c(FALSE, TRUE),
    laplace   = 0,
    adjust    = c(0.5, 1.0, 1.5)
)

nb_model <- train(
    x = X_train,
    y = y_train_fct,
    method = "naive_bayes",
    trControl = ctrl,
    metric = "ROC",
    tuneGrid = nb_grid
)

nb_pred <- predict(nb_model, X_test)
nb_prob <- predict(nb_model, X_test, type = "prob")
nb_cm <- confusionMatrix(nb_pred, y_test_fct, positive = "Win")

cat(sprintf(
    "\nNaive Bayes Results (trained in %.1fs):\nAccuracy: %.1f%%\nSensitivity: %.1f%%\nSpecificity: %.1f%%\nBest: usekernel=%s, adjust=%.1f\nCV AUC-ROC: %.3f",
    as.numeric(Sys.time() - t0, units = "secs"),
    nb_cm$overall["Accuracy"] * 100,
    nb_cm$byClass["Sensitivity"] * 100,
    nb_cm$byClass["Specificity"] * 100,
    as.character(nb_model$bestTune$usekernel),
    nb_model$bestTune$adjust,
    max(nb_model$results$ROC)
))

top_nb_features <- nb_imp$feature[1:8]

X_train %>%
    select(all_of(top_nb_features)) %>%
    mutate(outcome = y_train_fct) %>%
    pivot_longer(-outcome, names_to = "feature", values_to = "value") %>%
    mutate(feature = factor(feature, levels = top_nb_features)) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = value, fill = outcome, colour = outcome)) +
    geom_density(alpha = 0.35, linewidth = 0.4) +
    facet_wrap(~feature, scales = "free", ncol = 4) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("Loss" = "#e74c3c", "Win" = "#3498db")) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c("Loss" = "#e74c3c", "Win" = "#3498db")) +
    labs(

        x = NULL, y = "Density", fill = "Outcome", colour = "Outcome"
    ) +

The four resource differentials carry the widest class gap (golddiffat15 1.22 pooled sd, xpdiffat15 1.12, csdiffat15 1.00, kill_diff_15 0.98) and are roughly Gaussian, so the default likelihood fits them well. kda_15 is right-skewed, plate_diff is integer-discretised, and firsttower is binary - none Gaussian, which is why CV picks usekernel = TRUE. Every Win density sits to the right of its Loss density with substantial overlap around zero, so NB needs to combine many features to reach a sharp posterior - the source of its well-known push-to-extremes calibration behaviour.

9.7 KNN

Distance-based; runs on the standardised matrix. Multicollinearity inflates correlated dimensions in the Euclidean metric, so we expect KNN to lose ground to RF/CART here.

t0 <- Sys.time()

# k grid log-spaced from 5 to ~4*sqrt(n), forced odd to avoid 50/50 ties.
n_train <- nrow(X_train_scaled)
k_theo <- round(sqrt(n_train))
k_grid <- unique(round(exp(seq(log(5), log(k_theo * 4), length.out = 12))))
k_grid <- ifelse(k_grid %% 2 == 0, k_grid + 1, k_grid)

knn_model <- train(
    x = X_train_scaled,
    y = y_train_fct,
    method = "knn",
    trControl = ctrl,
    metric = "ROC",
    tuneGrid = expand.grid(k = k_grid)
)

knn_pred <- predict(knn_model, X_test_scaled)
knn_prob <- predict(knn_model, X_test_scaled, type = "prob")
knn_cm <- confusionMatrix(knn_pred, y_test_fct, positive = "Win")

cat(sprintf(
    "\nKNN Results (%.1fs):\nAccuracy: %.1f%%\nSensitivity (Win recall): %.1f%%\nSpecificity (Loss recall): %.1f%%\nBest k: %d\nCV AUC-ROC: %.3f",
    as.numeric(Sys.time() - t0, units = "secs"),
    knn_cm$overall["Accuracy"] * 100,
    knn_cm$byClass["Sensitivity"] * 100,
    knn_cm$byClass["Specificity"] * 100,
    knn_model$bestTune$k,
    max(knn_model$results$ROC)
))

9.8 Decision Tree CART

Single-tree analogue of RF; like RF, immune to multicollinearity. We tune the complexity parameter cp over {1e-5, 5e-5, 1e-4, 5e-4, 1e-3}.

t0 <- Sys.time()

# cp (complexity parameter) controls tree depth - tuned via 5-fold CV
cart_model <- train(
    x = X_train,
    y = y_train_fct,
    method = "rpart",
    trControl = ctrl,
    metric = "ROC",
    tuneGrid = expand.grid(cp = c(0.00001, 0.00005, 0.0001, 0.0005, 0.001))
)

cart_pred <- predict(cart_model, X_test)
cart_prob <- predict(cart_model, X_test, type = "prob")
cart_cm <- confusionMatrix(cart_pred, y_test_fct, positive = "Win")

cat(sprintf(
    "\nCART Results (%.1fs):\nAccuracy: %.1f%%\nSensitivity (Win recall): %.1f%%\nSpecificity (Loss recall): %.1f%%\nBest cp: %.4f\nCV AUC-ROC: %.3f",
    as.numeric(Sys.time() - t0, units = "secs"),
    cart_cm$overall["Accuracy"] * 100,
    cart_cm$byClass["Sensitivity"] * 100,
    cart_cm$byClass["Specificity"] * 100,
    cart_model$bestTune$cp,
    max(cart_model$results$ROC)
))

9.9 XGBoost

This model is used as the strongest non-linear baseline in the recent LoL prediction literature. Like RF and CART it is immune to multicollinearity and feature scaling. We tune nrounds, max_depth, and eta over a small grid; the remaining XGBoost hyperparameters are held at sensible defaults to keep the search tractable.

t0 <- Sys.time()

xgb_grid <- expand.grid(
    nrounds          = c(100, 300),
    max_depth        = c(4, 6),
    eta              = c(0.05, 0.1),
    gamma            = 0,
    colsample_bytree = 0.8,
    min_child_weight = 1,
    subsample        = 0.8
)

xgb_model <- train(
    x = X_train,
    y = y_train_fct,
    method = "xgbTree",
    trControl = ctrl,
    metric = "ROC",
    tuneGrid = xgb_grid,
    verbosity = 0
)

xgb_pred <- predict(xgb_model, X_test)
xgb_prob <- predict(xgb_model, X_test, type = "prob")
xgb_cm <- confusionMatrix(xgb_pred, y_test_fct, positive = "Win")

cat(sprintf(
    "\nXGBoost Results (trained in %.1fs):\nAccuracy: %.1f%%\nSensitivity (Win recall): %.1f%%\nSpecificity (Loss recall): %.1f%%\nBest nrounds=%d, max_depth=%d, eta=%.2f\nCV AUC-ROC: %.3f",
    as.numeric(Sys.time() - t0, units = "secs"),
    xgb_cm$overall["Accuracy"] * 100,
    xgb_cm$byClass["Sensitivity"] * 100,
    xgb_cm$byClass["Specificity"] * 100,
    xgb_model$bestTune$nrounds,
    xgb_model$bestTune$max_depth,
    xgb_model$bestTune$eta,
    max(xgb_model$results$ROC)
))

9.10 Model comparison

Side-by-side test-set metrics, confusion matrices, ROC curves. We check (a) which models beat the 72.9 % gold-rule baseline and (b) whether the non-linear RF gains anything over the linear/probabilistic baselines.

calc_metrics <- function(cm, prob, y_true, name) {
    roc_obj <- roc(y_true, prob[, "Win"], levels = c("Loss", "Win"), quiet = TRUE)
    tibble(
        Model = name,
        Accuracy = cm$overall["Accuracy"] * 100,
        AUC_ROC = auc(roc_obj) * 100,
        Precision = cm$byClass["Pos Pred Value"] * 100,
        Recall = cm$byClass["Sensitivity"] * 100,
        F1 = 2 * cm$byClass["Pos Pred Value"] * cm$byClass["Sensitivity"] /
            (cm$byClass["Pos Pred Value"] + cm$byClass["Sensitivity"]) * 100
    )
}

metrics <- bind_rows(
    calc_metrics(lr_cm, lr_prob, y_test_fct, "Logistic Regression"),
    calc_metrics(rf_cm, rf_prob, y_test_fct, "Random Forest"),
    calc_metrics(cart_cm, cart_prob, y_test_fct, "CART"),
    calc_metrics(nb_cm, nb_prob, y_test_fct, "Naive Bayes"),
    calc_metrics(knn_cm, knn_prob, y_test_fct, "KNN"),
    calc_metrics(xgb_cm, xgb_prob, y_test_fct, "XGBoost")
)

knitr::kable(metrics, digits = 1, caption = "Model Performance Comparison (H1)")

plot_cm <- function(cm, title) {
    cm_df <- as.data.frame(cm$table)
    ggplot(cm_df, aes(x = Reference, y = Prediction, fill = Freq)) +
        geom_tile() +
        geom_text(aes(label = Freq), size = 6) +
        scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "#3498db") +
        labs(title = title) +
        theme_minimal() +
        theme(
            legend.position = "none",
            plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
            panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA)
        )
}

    plot_cm(knn_cm, "KNN"),
    plot_cm(xgb_cm, "XGBoost"),
    ncol = 6
)

The test set inherits the underlying ~53/47 Blue-side base rate, so the ratio of TP to TN reflects how each model balances Win recall against Loss recall. Across all matrices, precision and recall stay within a few points of each other, which means F1 tracks accuracy closely and no model is systematically biased toward predicting Win or Loss.

roc_lr <- roc(y_test_fct, lr_prob[, "Win"], levels = c("Loss", "Win"), quiet = TRUE)
roc_rf <- roc(y_test_fct, rf_prob[, "Win"], levels = c("Loss", "Win"), quiet = TRUE)

9.11 Explainability comparison

Each model produces an importance score on a different axis (LR: coefficient magnitude, RF: mean Gini decrease, CART: total Gini reduction across splits, NB: filter-based per-feature AUC, XGBoost: split gain). KNN is excluded - no native importance signal. The interesting question is whether the five rankings agree on a small core of features.

# KNN excluded - no meaningful feature importance
top_features <- bind_rows(
    lr_coefs %>% mutate(rank = row_number(), model = "LR") %>%
        select(feature, rank, model),
    rf_imp %>% mutate(rank = row_number(), model = "RF") %>%
        select(feature, rank, model),
    cart_imp %>% mutate(rank = row_number(), model = "CART") %>%
        select(feature, rank, model),
    nb_imp %>% mutate(rank = row_number(), model = "NB") %>%
        select(feature, rank, model),
    xgb_imp %>% mutate(rank = row_number(), model = "XGB") %>%
        select(feature, rank, model)
)

ggplot(top_features, aes(x = reorder(feature, -rank), y = rank, color = model)) +
    geom_jitter(size = 3, width = 0, height = 0.2) +
    coord_flip() +
    scale_y_reverse(breaks = 1:max(top_features$rank)) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c("LR" = "#3498db", "RF" = "#27ae60", "CART" = "#9b59b6", "NB" = "#e67e22", "XGB" = "#16a085")) +
    labs(
        title = "Feature importance ranks per model",
        x = NULL, y = "Rank (1 = most important)", color = "Model"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()

Each importance metric measures something different, so the raw scores cannot be averaged across models. Ranks, however, are comparable: avg_rank summarises which features every method agrees on, and rank_spread flags where they diverge.

full_ranks <- lr_coefs %>%
    mutate(rank_LR = row_number()) %>%
    select(feature, rank_LR) %>%
    full_join(rf_imp %>% mutate(rank_RF = row_number()) %>% select(feature, rank_RF),
        by = "feature"
    ) %>%
    full_join(cart_imp %>% mutate(rank_CART = row_number()) %>% select(feature, rank_CART),
        by = "feature"
    ) %>%
    full_join(nb_imp %>% mutate(rank_NB = row_number()) %>% select(feature, rank_NB),
        by = "feature"
    ) %>%
    full_join(xgb_imp %>% mutate(rank_XGB = row_number()) %>% select(feature, rank_XGB),
        by = "feature"
    ) %>%
    mutate(
        avg_rank = rowMeans(across(starts_with("rank_")), na.rm = TRUE),
        rank_spread = apply(
            across(starts_with("rank_")), 1,
            function(r) max(r, na.rm = TRUE) - min(r, na.rm = TRUE)
        )
    ) %>%
    arrange(avg_rank)

knitr::kable(
    full_ranks,
    digits = 2,
    caption = "Cross-model feature ranks. Lower avg_rank = consistently important across methods; higher rank_spread = methods disagree."
)
Cross-model feature ranks. Lower avg_rank = consistently important across methods; higher rank_spread = methods disagree.
feature rank_LR rank_RF rank_CART rank_NB rank_XGB avg_rank rank_spread
golddiffat15 4 1 1 1 1 1.6 3
csdiffat15 1 3 3 3 4 2.8 3
xpdiffat15 8 2 2 2 3 3.4 6
winrate_diff 2 4 6 9 2 4.6 7
firsttower 5 10 4 8 5 6.4 6
kill_diff_15 6 9 5 4 11 7.0 7
kda_15 10 5 9 6 9 7.8 5
firstdragon 3 13 8 12 6 8.4 10
firstherald 7 12 7 10 7 8.6 5
assist_diff_15 9 8 10 7 10 8.8 3

The continuous early-game differentials - golddiffat15, xpdiffat15, csdiffat15, and winrate_diff - head every ranking with low avg_rank and small rank_spread, forming the consensus core that any defence of H1 should rely on. Disagreement concentrates on the binary objective flags firstdragon and firstherald, which rank high for Logistic Regression but low for the tree ensembles and the Naive Bayes filter. This is a metric-driven artefact: LR treats each flag as an additive log-odds shift, the tree models absorb the same signal into continuous splits, and the filter score reads the flags as weak standalone predictors. LASSO retains firstdragon with a non-zero coefficient in S3, which confirms that the disagreement reflects differences in measurement scale rather than a lack of substantive signal.

9.12 Same models, enriched data

H1 summarises the early game at the team level - one gold-diff per game, one xp-diff per game - but each match actually carries five values per metric, one per lane. Aggregating loses structure: a 1,000-gold team lead carried entirely by bot is a stronger signal than the same lead spread evenly across five lanes. We hold the S1 models and the train/test split fixed and refit them on an enriched matrix - H1 plus per-role @15 differentials for economy (gold, xp, cs) and combat (kills, assists, deaths) - to see whether the extra granularity beats the team aggregate.

# Per-role @15 differentials. Economy diffs come straight from the player row;
# combat diffs we compute as Blue-player-stat minus lane-opponent stat.
role_enriched <- players %>%
    filter(
        position %in% c("top", "jng", "mid", "bot", "sup"),
        side == "Blue"
    ) %>%
    mutate(
        killdiffat15   = killsat15 - opp_killsat15,
        assistdiffat15 = assistsat15 - opp_assistsat15,
        deathdiffat15  = deathsat15 - opp_deathsat15
    ) %>%
    select(
        gameid, position,
        golddiffat15, xpdiffat15, csdiffat15,
        killdiffat15, assistdiffat15, deathdiffat15
    ) %>%
    drop_na() %>%
    pivot_wider(
        id_cols = gameid,
        names_from = position,
        values_from = c(
            golddiffat15, xpdiffat15, csdiffat15,
            killdiffat15, assistdiffat15, deathdiffat15
        ),
        names_glue = "{position}_{.value}"
    )

games_enriched <- games_model %>%
    inner_join(role_enriched, by = "gameid") %>%
    drop_na()

cat(sprintf(
    "Per-role features added: %d (5 roles x 6 metrics @15)\nGames after join + drop_na: %d (lost %d rows from H1, %.1f%%)\nFeature count: %d (was %d on H1)\n",
    ncol(role_enriched) - 1,
    nrow(games_enriched),
    nrow(games_model) - nrow(games_enriched),
    (nrow(games_model) - nrow(games_enriched)) / nrow(games_model) * 100,
    ncol(games_enriched) - 2,
    ncol(games_model) - 2
))
Per-role features added: 30 (5 roles x 6 metrics @15)
Games after join + drop_na: 9236 (lost 0 rows from H1, 0.0%)
Feature count: 44 (was 14 on H1)
# Reuse train_ids so the only thing changing between runs is the feature matrix.
train_e <- games_enriched %>%
    filter(gameid %in% train_ids) %>%
    select(-gameid)
test_e <- games_enriched %>%
    filter(!gameid %in% train_ids) %>%
    select(-gameid)

X_train_e <- train_e %>% select(-blue_win)
X_test_e <- test_e %>% select(-blue_win)
y_train_e <- factor(train_e$blue_win, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("Loss", "Win"))
y_test_e <- factor(test_e$blue_win, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("Loss", "Win"))

preproc_e <- preProcess(X_train_e, method = c("center", "scale"))
X_train_e_scaled <- predict(preproc_e, X_train_e)
X_test_e_scaled <- predict(preproc_e, X_test_e)

The 30 per-role columns sum (per metric) to the team-level totals already in H1, so the enriched matrix is rank-deficient by construction (top + jng + mid + bot + sup ≡ team for gold, XP, CS, kills, and assists; only the death-diff family escapes because S1 deliberately omitted death_diff_15). A naive solve(cor(X)) therefore fails with a singular matrix. We first identify and drop the exact linear combinations with caret::findLinearCombos(), then iteratively remove the feature with the largest VIF until every remaining VIF is at or below 10. Working on the trimmed matrix removes the redundancy that would otherwise dominate the comparison with H1 and lets each model fit on a feature set whose coefficients (LR) and split candidates (RF/XGB) are no longer aliased.

# Step 1: drop the 5 columns that are exact linear combinations of others
lc_e <- caret::findLinearCombos(as.matrix(X_train_e_scaled))
removed_perfect <- names(X_train_e_scaled)[lc_e$remove]
keep1 <- setdiff(seq_len(ncol(X_train_e_scaled)), lc_e$remove)
X_iter <- X_train_e_scaled[, keep1]

# Step 2: iteratively drop the max-VIF feature while max(VIF) > 10
threshold_e <- 10
removed_vif <- character()
repeat {
    vif <- diag(solve(cor(X_iter)))
    if (max(vif) <= threshold_e) break
    drop <- names(vif)[which.max(vif)]
    removed_vif <- c(removed_vif, drop)
    X_iter <- X_iter[, setdiff(names(X_iter), drop)]
}
surviving_features_e <- names(X_iter)

cat(sprintf(
    "Started: %d features\nDropped (perfect collinearity): %d -> %s\nDropped (iterative VIF > %d): %d -> %s\nSurviving feature count: %d\n",
    ncol(X_train_e_scaled),
    length(removed_perfect), paste(removed_perfect, collapse = ", "),
    threshold_e,
    length(removed_vif),     paste(removed_vif, collapse = ", "),
    length(surviving_features_e)
))

Surviving feature count: 31

X_test_e <- X_test_e[, surviving_features_e]

lr_e <- train(
    x = X_train_e_scaled, y = y_train_e,
    method = "glm", family = "binomial",
    trControl = ctrl, metric = "ROC"
)

# RF mtry grid scaled to the new feature count.
n_feat_e <- ncol(X_train_e)
rf_grid_e <- unique(round(c(
    sqrt(n_feat_e), sqrt(n_feat_e) * 1.5,
    sqrt(n_feat_e) * 2, sqrt(n_feat_e) * 3
)))
rf_e <- train(
    x = X_train_e, y = y_train_e,
    method = "rf", trControl = ctrl, metric = "ROC",
    tuneGrid = expand.grid(mtry = rf_grid_e), ntree = 500
)

nb_e <- train(
    x = X_train_e, y = y_train_e,
    method = "naive_bayes", trControl = ctrl, metric = "ROC",
    tuneGrid = nb_grid
)

n_train_e <- nrow(X_train_e_scaled)
k_theo_e <- round(sqrt(n_train_e))
k_grid_e <- unique(round(exp(seq(log(5), log(k_theo_e * 4), length.out = 12))))
k_grid_e <- ifelse(k_grid_e %% 2 == 0, k_grid_e + 1, k_grid_e)
knn_e <- train(
    x = X_train_e_scaled, y = y_train_e,
    method = "knn", trControl = ctrl, metric = "ROC",
    tuneGrid = expand.grid(k = k_grid_e)
)

cart_e <- train(
    x = X_train_e, y = y_train_e,
    method = "rpart", trControl = ctrl, metric = "ROC",
    tuneGrid = expand.grid(cp = c(0.00001, 0.00005, 0.0001, 0.0005, 0.001))
)

xgb_e <- train(
    x = X_train_e, y = y_train_e,
    method = "xgbTree", trControl = ctrl, metric = "ROC",

)
score_e <- function(model, X_eval, name) {
    cls <- predict(model, X_eval)
    prob <- predict(model, X_eval, type = "prob")
    cm <- confusionMatrix(cls, y_test_e, positive = "Win")
    calc_metrics(cm, prob, y_test_e, name)
}

    score_e(nb_e, X_test_e, "Naive Bayes"),
    score_e(knn_e, X_test_e_scaled, "KNN"),

)

With multicollinearity removed, the trimmed enriched matrix matches the H1 baseline. Mean AUC -0.16 pp, mean accuracy +0.10 pp, 4 of 6 models improve. The trim is what makes the comparison fair - on the raw 44-feature enrichment every model paid a penalty for the redundant gold/XP/CS aliases, with NB hit hardest by the top + jng + mid + bot + sup ≡ team identities.

  • LR: +0.14 AUC - coefficients no longer split across the aliased gold/XP duplicates; surviving per-role columns add only marginal signal.
  • RF: +0.59 AUC - tuned mtry rises from 3 to 6, but the ceiling is unchanged.
  • NB: -0.62 AUC - independence assumption is now satisfied (VIF ≤ 10); the residual loss is the per-role columns adding noise rather than signal.
  • KNN: +0.10 AUC - 31 standardised dimensions stay Euclidean-comparable; k = 345 smooths over local noise.
  • CART: -1.26 AUC, +0.65 pp accuracy - single-tree variance is sensitive to the wider input regardless of VIF cleanup.

Bottom line: team-level totals already saturate the @15 signal, so H1 stays as the S1 reference set (S3 selection, Shiny export). H2 below asks the sharper question - does bot lane specifically carry signal beyond the team aggregates? Of the five per-role gold-diff columns, only bot_golddiffat15 survives the VIF filter, so a non-trivial bot-lane importance is not an alias artefact.

9.12.1 Role-feature importance (H2 test)

H2 asks whether bot lane carries the strongest role-specific early-game signal. The AUC half of the test is the enriched-vs-H1 RF comparison in the delta table above. The role-ranking half is sharper after the VIF trim: of the original 30 per-role columns, 22 survive (the others were either perfect linear combinations of the team totals or had VIF > 10 against the rest of the matrix). H2 is supported if and only if the top-ranked bot_* feature in the enriched RF outranks the best surviving feature of every other role.

enr_imp <- varImp(rf_e)$importance %>%
    rownames_to_column("feature") %>%
    arrange(desc(Overall))

role_features <- enr_imp %>%
    filter(str_detect(feature, "^(top|jng|mid|bot|sup)_"))

ggplot(
    enr_imp %>% head(25),
    aes(
        x = reorder(feature, Overall), y = Overall,
        fill = str_detect(feature, "^(top|jng|mid|bot|sup)_")
    )
) +
    geom_col() +
    coord_flip() +
    scale_fill_manual(
        values = c("FALSE" = "#95a5a6", "TRUE" = "#e74c3c"),
        labels = c("Team-level", "Role-specific")
    ) +
    labs(
        title = sprintf(
            "Trimmed enriched RF - feature importances (top %d of %d, H2 test)",
            min(25, nrow(enr_imp)), nrow(enr_imp)
        ),
        x = NULL, y = "Importance", fill = "Feature type"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()
bot_features <- role_features %>%
    filter(str_detect(feature, "^bot_")) %>%
    mutate(overall_rank = match(feature, enr_imp$feature))

other_role_features <- role_features %>%
    filter(!str_detect(feature, "^bot_")) %>%
    group_by(role = str_extract(feature, "^[a-z]+")) %>%
    summarise(
        best_rank = min(match(feature, enr_imp$feature)),
        avg_importance = mean(Overall),
        .groups = "drop"
    )

The VIF trim makes this an honest comparison - bot_golddiffat15 is the only per-role gold-diff column to clear the threshold, so a bot-lane top rank cannot be driven by an aliased team-level total.

10 Scenario 3: Feature Selection

Scenario 3 reduces the 14 candidate early-game predictors to a more interpretable subset. The S1 VIF analysis flagged residual collinearity on golddiffat15 and kill_diff_15, and the LR coefficient table left several features carrying near-zero weight - both are signs that some of the 14 predictors duplicate signal already captured by the dominant resource diffs. We compare one algorithmic method (forward stepwise via AIC) with two embedded regularisation methods (LASSO, Elastic Net) to identify which predictors are consistently retained and whether a compact subset can match the full model’s predictive performance.

10.1 Forward Stepwise (AIC)

Forward stepwise selection starts from an intercept-only model and admits one feature at a time, each time choosing the feature whose addition lowers AIC by the most, and stopping when no remaining candidate can lower AIC further. We use it on the 14 H1 features and track per-step Wald p-values to see when individual evidence weakens as correlated predictors enter.

t0 <- Sys.time()

fwd_train_df <- as.data.frame(X_train_scaled)
fwd_train_df$result <- y_train_fct
fwd_test_df <- as.data.frame(X_test_scaled)

null_model <- glm(result ~ 1, data = fwd_train_df, family = "binomial")
full_formula <- as.formula(
    paste("result ~", paste(names(X_train_scaled), collapse = " + "))
)

set.seed(42)
fwd_model <- MASS::stepAIC(
    null_model,
    scope     = list(lower = null_model, upper = full_formula),
    direction = "forward",
    trace     = FALSE
)

fwd_selected <- names(coef(fwd_model))
fwd_selected <- fwd_selected[fwd_selected != "(Intercept)"]
fwd_n <- length(fwd_selected)
fwd_eliminated <- setdiff(colnames(X_train_scaled), fwd_selected)

# Reconstruct addition order from stepAIC's anova trace
fwd_anova <- fwd_model$anova
fwd_addition_order <- gsub("^\\+ ", "", as.character(fwd_anova$Step))
fwd_addition_order <- fwd_addition_order[fwd_addition_order != ""]

fwd_pred_prob_raw <- predict(fwd_model, newdata = fwd_test_df, type = "response")
fwd_pred_class <- factor(ifelse(fwd_pred_prob_raw > 0.5, "Win", "Loss"),
    levels = c("Loss", "Win")
)
fwd_cm <- confusionMatrix(fwd_pred_class, y_test_fct, positive = "Win")
fwd_roc <- roc(y_test_fct, fwd_pred_prob_raw,
    levels = c("Loss", "Win"), quiet = TRUE
)

cat(sprintf(
    "\nForward Stepwise Results (%.1fs):\nFeatures selected: %d / %d\nFinal AIC: %.1f\nAccuracy:              %.1f%%\nSensitivity (Win recall):  %.1f%%\nSpecificity (Loss recall): %.1f%%\nAUC-ROC (test):        %.3f",
    as.numeric(Sys.time() - t0, units = "secs"),
    fwd_n, ncol(X_train_scaled),
    AIC(fwd_model),
    fwd_cm$overall["Accuracy"] * 100,
    fwd_cm$byClass["Sensitivity"] * 100,
    fwd_cm$byClass["Specificity"] * 100,
    auc(fwd_roc)
))

Forward stepwise keeps 10 of the 14 features and matches the full-model LR baseline (test AUC 0.842 vs 0.842, accuracy 75.6% vs 75.5%). The four dropped features - assist_diff_15, firstblood, gold_efficiency_15, plate_diff - are collectively redundant with the rest of the matrix.

golddiffat15 enters first and drops AIC by ~2,400 on its own - more than every subsequent admission combined. The curve plateaus by k = 7; the last three admissions clear AIC by deviance drops under four units each - the boundary of the criterion, and the band where the p-value evidence is weakest.

10.2 Significance evolution along the addition path

# At each subset size k, refit glm on the first k features (in addition order)
# and capture coefficient + SE + p-value for every feature in the model.
fwd_signif_path <- map_dfr(seq_along(fwd_addition_order), function(k) {
    feats <- fwd_addition_order[seq_len(k)]
    df_k <- fwd_train_df[, c(feats, "result"), drop = FALSE]
    m_k <- glm(result ~ ., data = df_k, family = "binomial")
    s_k <- summary(m_k)$coefficients
    s_k <- s_k[rownames(s_k) != "(Intercept)", , drop = FALSE]
    tibble(
        step    = k,
        feature = rownames(s_k),
        coef    = s_k[, "Estimate"],
        se      = s_k[, "Std. Error"],
        p_value = s_k[, "Pr(>|z|)"]
    )
})

fwd_pvalue_table <- fwd_signif_path %>%
    select(step, feature, p_value) %>%
    pivot_wider(names_from = step, values_from = p_value, names_prefix = "k=") %>%
    mutate(feature = factor(feature, levels = fwd_addition_order)) %>%
    arrange(feature)

fwd_pvalue_display <- fwd_pvalue_table %>%
    mutate(across(
        starts_with("k="),
        ~ ifelse(is.na(.x), "-",
            ifelse(.x < 0.001, "<0.001", sprintf("%.3f", .x))
        )
    ))

knitr::kable(
    fwd_pvalue_display,
    caption = sprintf(
        "P-value evolution across the addition path (k = subset size, %d steps total). Each row is a retained feature in order of admission; each column is the model with that many predictors. Cells where a feature has not yet entered are blank.",
        fwd_n
    ),
    align = c("l", rep("r", fwd_n))
)

fwd_signif_summary <- fwd_signif_path %>%
    group_by(feature) %>%
    summarise(
        added_at = min(step),
        max_p = max(p_value),
        final_p = p_value[step == max(step)],
        ever_lost = any(p_value > 0.05),
        .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    mutate(feature = factor(feature, levels = fwd_addition_order)) %>%
    arrange(feature)

fwd_signif_display <- fwd_signif_summary %>%
    transmute(
        feature,
        added_at,
        max_p_value = ifelse(max_p < 0.001, "<0.001", sprintf("%.3f", max_p)),
        final_p_value = ifelse(final_p < 0.001, "<0.001", sprintf("%.3f", final_p)),
        ever_above_0.05 = ifelse(ever_lost, "yes", "no")
    )

ggplot(fwd_signif_plot_df, aes(x = step, y = neg_log_p, color = feature, group = feature)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +

        x = "Subset size (k)",

        panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
