Two patterns are visible in the plot. First, every feature enters with a very small p-value - -log10(p) above the dashed 0.05 line by a wide margin - and most stay rock-solid throughout (winrate_diff and the three first-objective flags barely move). Second, two features show clear decay as their collinearity partners are admitted: golddiffat15 drops sharply once csdiffat15 enters at k = 6, and kill_diff_15 drops once xpdiffat15 enters at k = 8. Both still finish significant, but the trajectory shows their evidence being absorbed by the partner predictor. The only feature that ends below the threshold is kda_15, admitted last with a final p-value of 0.051 - the case where AIC and individual significance disagree: it improves the joint fit enough to be admitted, but its standalone coefficient evidence is at the edge.

10.3 LASSO (L1)

LASSO adds an L1 penalty to logistic regression, shrinking each coefficient toward zero proportionally to λ and driving weak ones to exactly zero - selection and estimation happen in the same step. It is directly motivated by the VIF findings from S1: features like assist_diff_15 and kill_diff_15 share most of their signal with golddiffat15, and L1 is the standard way to resolve that redundancy.

lambda is tuned with cv.glmnet (5-fold CV over ~100 values). We select lambda.1se - the largest λ within one standard error of the CV minimum - because it gives a sparser model statistically indistinguishable from the best-fitting one.

t0 <- Sys.time()

set.seed(42)
lasso_cv <- cv.glmnet(
    x            = as.matrix(X_train_scaled),
    y            = y_train,
    alpha        = 1,
    family       = "binomial",
    nfolds       = 5,
    type.measure = "auc"
)

# lambda.1se: the largest lambda within 1 SE of the minimum - gives a sparser model
# that is nearly as accurate as lambda.min but keeps fewer features
lasso_coefs <- coef(lasso_cv, s = "lambda.1se")

lasso_coef_df <- data.frame(
    feature = rownames(lasso_coefs),
    coefficient = as.numeric(lasso_coefs)
) %>%
    filter(feature != "(Intercept)") %>%
    arrange(desc(abs(coefficient)))

lasso_selected <- lasso_coef_df %>% filter(coefficient != 0)
lasso_eliminated <- lasso_coef_df %>% filter(coefficient == 0)

lasso_pred_prob <- predict(lasso_cv,
    newx = as.matrix(X_test_scaled),
    s = "lambda.1se", type = "response"
)
lasso_pred_class <- factor(ifelse(lasso_pred_prob > 0.5, "Win", "Loss"),
    levels = c("Loss", "Win")
)
lasso_cm <- confusionMatrix(lasso_pred_class, y_test_fct, positive = "Win")
lasso_roc <- roc(y_test_fct, as.numeric(lasso_pred_prob),
    levels = c("Loss", "Win"), quiet = TRUE
)

cat(sprintf(
    "\nLASSO Results (%.1fs):\nLambda (1se): %.6f\nFeatures kept: %d / %d (eliminated %d)\nAccuracy: %.1f%%\nSensitivity (Win recall): %.1f%%\nSpecificity (Loss recall): %.1f%%\nAUC-ROC: %.3f",
    as.numeric(Sys.time() - t0, units = "secs"),
    lasso_cv$lambda.1se,
    nrow(lasso_selected), nrow(lasso_coef_df), nrow(lasso_eliminated),
    lasso_cm$overall["Accuracy"] * 100,
    lasso_cm$byClass["Sensitivity"] * 100,
    lasso_cm$byClass["Specificity"] * 100,
    auc(lasso_roc)
))

    ) +

    ) +
    annotate("text",
        x = log(lasso_cv$lambda.min), y = max(cv_df$cvm),

    ) +
    annotate("text",
        x = log(lasso_cv$lambda.1se), y = max(cv_df$cvm),
        label = "lambda.1se", hjust = -0.1, color = "#2ecc71", size = 3.5
    ) +
    labs(
        title = "LASSO: CV AUC vs log(λ)",
        subtitle = "Green = lambda.1se (chosen), Red = lambda.min",

    theme_minimal()
lasso_selected %>%
    mutate(feature = reorder(feature, abs(coefficient))) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = feature, y = coefficient, fill = coefficient > 0)) +
    geom_col() +
    coord_flip() +
    scale_fill_manual(
        values = c("TRUE" = "#2ecc71", "FALSE" = "#e74c3c"),

        subtitle = "Ranked by absolute coefficient - longer bar = stronger signal",
        x = NULL, y = "Coefficient", fill = "Direction"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()

LASSO retained 7 of the 14 features at lambda.1se = 0.040 and achieved AUC-ROC of 0.839 with 75.0% accuracy - within 0.3 pp of the full-model baseline while halving the feature count. We chose lambda.1se because it sits at the point where the curve begins to rise - the last position where a sparser model is statistically indistinguishable from the best-fitting one.

The combat features kill_diff_15 and assist_diff_15 were zeroed out, consistent with the VIF analysis: kills and assists translate directly into team gold, so their signal is already captured by golddiffat15 once L1 pressure is applied. The two ratio features were also eliminated - gold_efficiency_15 = goldat15 / csat15 overlaps with golddiffat15 and csdiffat15, and kda_15 overlaps with the combat differentials. plate_diff and grub_diff are absorbed by the dominant economic core; their univariate signal is real but redundant. firstblood was also eliminated - consistent with the EDA, securing the first kill adds no predictive value once the full 15-minute economic picture is present.

The 7 retained features form a coherent minimal set: the three resource differentials (golddiffat15, xpdiffat15, csdiffat15) capture the economic picture at 15 minutes, winrate_diff adds pre-game team quality, and the three first-objective flags (firsttower, firstdragon, firstherald) contribute a separate structural layer. All surviving coefficients are positive: being ahead in any of these dimensions increases the Blue team’s win probability.

10.4 Elastic Net (L1 + L2)

We apply Elastic Net as the second embedded method because our predictors include groups of correlated variables that may still carry complementary information. LASSO can be unstable under strong collinearity - it may arbitrarily keep one variable from a correlated group and zero the rest - which is a concern given the resource differential cluster in our data.

Elastic Net combines L1 and L2 regularisation, allowing it to perform feature selection while also handling correlated predictors more smoothly than pure LASSO. This makes it useful for checking whether features removed by LASSO are truly redundant, or whether they still contribute secondary signal when correlated variables are allowed to share predictive weight.

The blend between L1 and L2 is controlled by alpha (0 = pure Ridge, 1 = pure LASSO). We search the full alpha range in 0.05 steps, using the same fixed cross-validation folds across all alphas so the resulting CV AUC values are directly comparable. The alpha whose lambda.1se model maximises 5-fold CV AUC is selected as the final model; if the AUC curve is flat across alphas, the data cannot distinguish LASSO from Ridge at this sample size and the L1/L2 mix is effectively underdetermined.

t0 <- Sys.time()

alpha_grid <- seq(0, 1, by = 0.05)

# Fix fold assignments across all alphas so cv_auc values are directly comparable
set.seed(42)
fold_ids <- sample(rep(seq(5), length.out = length(y_train)))

enet_cv_results <- map_dfr(alpha_grid, function(a) {
    cv_fit <- cv.glmnet(
        x            = as.matrix(X_train_scaled),
        y            = y_train,
        alpha        = a,
        family       = "binomial",
        foldid       = fold_ids,
        type.measure = "auc"
    )
    idx_1se <- cv_fit$index["1se", 1]
    n_kept <- sum(coef(cv_fit, s = "lambda.1se") != 0) - 1
    tibble(
        alpha      = a,
        lambda_1se = cv_fit$lambda.1se,
        cv_auc     = cv_fit$cvm[idx_1se],
        cv_auc_se  = cv_fit$cvsd[idx_1se],
        n_features = n_kept
    )
})

best_row <- enet_cv_results %>%
    arrange(desc(cv_auc)) %>%
    dplyr::slice(1)
best_alpha <- best_row$alpha
best_auc <- best_row$cv_auc
best_se <- best_row$cv_auc_se
within_1se <- enet_cv_results %>% filter(cv_auc >= best_auc - best_se)

cat(sprintf(
    "\nAlpha grid diagnostic: %d of %d alphas sit within 1 SE of the best CV AUC (%.3f >= %.3f).\n",
    nrow(within_1se), nrow(enet_cv_results), best_auc, best_auc - best_se
))

Alpha grid diagnostic: 21 of 21 alphas sit within 1 SE of the best CV AUC (0.839 >= 0.833).
cat(sprintf(
    "Alphas within 1 SE: %s\n",
    paste(sprintf("%.2f", within_1se$alpha), collapse = ", ")
))
Alphas within 1 SE: 0.00, 0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20, 0.25, 0.30, 0.35, 0.40, 0.45, 0.50, 0.55, 0.60, 0.65, 0.70, 0.75, 0.80, 0.85, 0.90, 0.95, 1.00
if (nrow(within_1se) >= nrow(enet_cv_results) - 2) {
    cat("-> CV AUC curve is effectively flat across alpha; the L1/L2 mix is underdetermined by this data.\n")
}
-> CV AUC curve is effectively flat across alpha; the L1/L2 mix is underdetermined by this data.
cat(sprintf("Best alpha: %.2f (CV AUC = %.4f)\n", best_alpha, best_auc))
Best alpha: 0.90 (CV AUC = 0.8386)
enet_cv_final <- cv.glmnet(
    x            = as.matrix(X_train_scaled),
    y            = y_train,
    alpha        = best_alpha,
    family       = "binomial",
    foldid       = fold_ids,
    type.measure = "auc"
)

enet_coef_raw <- coef(enet_cv_final, s = "lambda.1se")
enet_coef_df <- data.frame(
    feature     = rownames(enet_coef_raw),
    coefficient = as.numeric(enet_coef_raw)
) %>%
    filter(feature != "(Intercept)") %>%
    arrange(desc(abs(coefficient)))

enet_selected_df <- enet_coef_df %>% filter(coefficient != 0)
enet_selected <- enet_selected_df$feature

enet_pred_prob <- predict(enet_cv_final,
    newx = as.matrix(X_test_scaled),
    s = "lambda.1se", type = "response"
)
enet_pred_class <- factor(ifelse(enet_pred_prob > 0.5, "Win", "Loss"),
    levels = c("Loss", "Win")
)
enet_cm <- confusionMatrix(enet_pred_class, y_test_fct, positive = "Win")
enet_roc <- roc(y_test_fct, as.numeric(enet_pred_prob), levels = c("Loss", "Win"), quiet = TRUE)

cat(sprintf(
    "\nElastic Net Results (%.1fs):\nBest alpha: %.2f (0=Ridge, 1=LASSO)\nLambda (1se): %.6f\nFeatures kept: %d / %d (eliminated %d)\nAccuracy: %.1f%%\nSensitivity (Win recall): %.1f%%\nSpecificity (Loss recall): %.1f%%\nAUC-ROC: %.3f",
    as.numeric(Sys.time() - t0, units = "secs"),
    best_alpha,
    enet_cv_final$lambda.1se,
    nrow(enet_selected_df), nrow(enet_coef_df), nrow(enet_coef_df) - nrow(enet_selected_df),
    enet_cm$overall["Accuracy"] * 100,
    enet_cm$byClass["Sensitivity"] * 100,
    enet_cm$byClass["Specificity"] * 100,
    auc(enet_roc)
))

The CV AUC curve is almost flat across the entire alpha grid - all 21 tested values sit within 1 SE of the best AUC (0.839), and the wide confidence band suggests that differences between alphas are noise rather than signal. The dashed line marks the best AUC - 1 SE threshold; every alpha clears it comfortably, meaning no mixing ratio offers a statistically meaningful advantage over any other.

alpha = 0.90 (near-LASSO) achieves the highest point estimate, but the margin over other alphas is negligible. The correlated resource differentials do not cause the instability Elastic Net is designed to address - LASSO handles them as well as any Ridge blend at this sample size. Elastic Net keeps one feature beyond the LASSO core (kill_diff_15, the partner of the high-VIF golddiffat15 pair), reflecting the slightly weaker L1 pressure at α = 0.90. The downstream LR fits on the LASSO and Elastic Net subsets land within 0.05 pp AUC of each other, confirming that this 8th feature carries no predictive value beyond the consensus 7.

        feature_label = reorder(feature_label, n_methods),
        method        = factor(method, levels = c("Forward", "LASSO", "ElasticNet"))
    )

All three methods land within 0.3 pp AUC of the 14-feature LR baseline (84.2%) while using between 7 and 10 features: Forward 10 features at AUC 84.2%, ElasticNet 8 features at AUC 84.0%, LASSO 7 features at AUC 83.9%. The leanest model loses 0.3 pp AUC for half the feature count, so the four-to-seven features that the more aggressive selectors drop add at most 0.3 pp of joint signal.

10.6 S3 findings

Seven features are picked by all three methods, the consensus core: golddiffat15, xpdiffat15, csdiffat15, firsttower, firstdragon, firstherald, winrate_diff. This matches the EDA correlation ranking and the S1 cross-model importance consensus exactly. The three resource differentials at 15 minutes carry the largest share of signal - who is ahead in gold, XP, and CS is the dominant predictor. The three first-objective flags add a separate structural layer; first tower and first herald showed the strongest binary win-rate correlations in the EDA, and all three flags survive every selection criterion here. winrate_diff adds pre-game team quality independent of the in-game snapshot.

One feature falls in the “exactly two methods” band. kill_diff_15 is kept by Forward and Elastic Net but dropped by pure LASSO. It is the partner of the high-VIF cluster identified in S1: its standalone signal is real (Wald p < 0.001 in the forward fit), but most of it is captured by golddiffat15 once a strict L1 penalty is applied. Elastic Net’s small Ridge blend at α = 0.90 spares it; pure LASSO does not. Forward keeps it because admitting it lowers AIC by ~26 units - a clear improvement, even though the same predictive content can be cheaply absorbed by golddiffat15 under regularisation.

Two features are kept only by Forward: grub_diff and kda_15. Both are admitted at the very end of the addition path, with deviance drops just below four units each. The p-value evolution table shows that grub_diff retains marginal significance (final p = 0.041) while kda_15 slips just over the threshold (final p = 0.051) - both sit at the boundary of the AIC criterion and would not survive an L1 penalty.

Four features are never selected by any method: assist_diff_15, firstblood, gold_efficiency_15, plate_diff. Their coefficients in the unpenalised LR fit are small, and they offer no improvement strong enough to clear AIC, L1, or the mixed L1/L2 criterion. firstblood is the strongest null result: despite its prominence in esports commentary, its 400 gold value is negligible relative to a 15-minute lead, and the EDA already showed it produced the weakest binary win-rate shift of any objective flag. assist_diff_15 overlaps with the combat-and-economy core already covered by golddiffat15 and kill_diff_15; gold_efficiency_15 is a ratio of two features already in the model; plate_diff is an early-game objective signal already absorbed by the resource lead it helped produce.

11 Validation: best parametric S1 model on the S3-selected feature subsets

We refit Logistic Regression - the top S1 parametric learner (test AUC 0.842) - on each S3-selected subset to check whether the choice of selection method matters downstream. Same caret setup as S1 (5-fold CV, metric = "ROC", scaled inputs); only the feature matrix changes.

t0 <- Sys.time()

fit_lr_subset <- function(features) {
    X_tr <- X_train_scaled[, features, drop = FALSE]
    X_te <- X_test_scaled[, features, drop = FALSE]
    set.seed(42)
    fit <- train(
        x         = X_tr,
        y         = y_train_fct,
        method    = "glm",
        family    = "binomial",
        trControl = ctrl,
        metric    = "ROC"
    )
    pred <- predict(fit, X_te)
    prob <- predict(fit, X_te, type = "prob")
    cm <- confusionMatrix(pred, y_test_fct, positive = "Win")
    roc_obj <- roc(y_test_fct, prob[, "Win"],
        levels = c("Loss", "Win"), quiet = TRUE
    )
    list(fit = fit, cm = cm, roc = roc_obj, n = length(features))
}

lr_fwd <- fit_lr_subset(fwd_selected)
lr_lasso <- fit_lr_subset(lasso_selected$feature)
lr_enet <- fit_lr_subset(enet_selected)

cat(sprintf(
    "\nFitted three reduced-feature LR variants in %.1fs.\n",
    as.numeric(Sys.time() - t0, units = "secs")
))

All three reduced-feature LRs land within 0.3 pp AUC of the 14-feature baseline (0.842): Forward 0.842 (10 features), Elastic Net 0.840 (8), LASSO 0.839 (7). The four ROC curves overlap almost exactly, so any practical decision threshold transfers between subsets. The 7-feature LASSO model is the cheapest hit on the AUC ceiling, and the 0.3 pp gap to the full model is small enough that parsimony - coefficient interpretability and drift-robustness - is the better trade.

12 Cross-validation grid: every S1 model on every S3 selection

We extend the LR-specific validation to all six S1 learners by refitting each on every S3 subset (plus the full 14-feature baseline) under the S1 tuning grids. Naive Bayes is the model of interest here: its independence assumption is the one most directly violated by the correlated 15-minute differentials, so reduction should help it more than any other learner.

t0 <- Sys.time()

fit_model_subset <- function(model_name, features) {
    X_tr <- X_train[, features, drop = FALSE]
    X_te <- X_test[, features, drop = FALSE]
    X_tr_s <- X_train_scaled[, features, drop = FALSE]
    X_te_s <- X_test_scaled[, features, drop = FALSE]
    n_feat <- length(features)

    if (model_name == "LR") {
        set.seed(42)
        fit <- train(
            x = X_tr_s, y = y_train_fct, method = "glm", family = "binomial",
            trControl = ctrl, metric = "ROC"
        )
        prob <- predict(fit, X_te_s, type = "prob")
        pred <- predict(fit, X_te_s)
    } else if (model_name == "RF") {
        mtry_grid <- unique(pmin(c(2, 5, 7, 10, 15, 19), n_feat))
        set.seed(42)
        fit <- train(
            x = X_tr, y = y_train_fct, method = "rf",
            trControl = ctrl, metric = "ROC",
            tuneGrid = expand.grid(mtry = mtry_grid), ntree = 500
        )
        prob <- predict(fit, X_te, type = "prob")
        pred <- predict(fit, X_te)
    } else if (model_name == "NB") {
        set.seed(42)
        fit <- train(
            x = X_tr, y = y_train_fct, method = "naive_bayes",
            trControl = ctrl, metric = "ROC",
            tuneGrid = expand.grid(
                usekernel = c(FALSE, TRUE), laplace = 0,
                adjust = c(0.5, 1.0, 1.5)
            )
        )
        prob <- predict(fit, X_te, type = "prob")
        pred <- predict(fit, X_te)
    } else if (model_name == "KNN") {
        k_theo <- round(sqrt(nrow(X_tr_s)))
        k_grid <- unique(round(exp(seq(log(5), log(k_theo * 4), length.out = 12))))
        k_grid <- ifelse(k_grid %% 2 == 0, k_grid + 1, k_grid)
        set.seed(42)
        fit <- train(
            x = X_tr_s, y = y_train_fct, method = "knn",
            trControl = ctrl, metric = "ROC",
            tuneGrid = expand.grid(k = k_grid)
        )
        prob <- predict(fit, X_te_s, type = "prob")
        pred <- predict(fit, X_te_s)
    } else if (model_name == "CART") {
        set.seed(42)
        fit <- train(
            x = X_tr, y = y_train_fct, method = "rpart",
            trControl = ctrl, metric = "ROC",
            tuneGrid = expand.grid(cp = c(1e-5, 5e-5, 1e-4, 5e-4, 1e-3))
        )
        prob <- predict(fit, X_te, type = "prob")
        pred <- predict(fit, X_te)
    } else if (model_name == "XGBoost") {
        set.seed(42)
        fit <- train(
            x = X_tr, y = y_train_fct, method = "xgbTree",
            trControl = ctrl, metric = "ROC", verbosity = 0,
            tuneGrid = expand.grid(
                nrounds = c(100, 300), max_depth = c(4, 6),
                eta = c(0.05, 0.1), gamma = 0,
                colsample_bytree = 0.8,
                min_child_weight = 1, subsample = 0.8
            )
        )
        prob <- predict(fit, X_te, type = "prob")
        pred <- predict(fit, X_te)
    }

    cm <- confusionMatrix(pred, y_test_fct, positive = "Win")
    rc <- roc(y_test_fct, prob[, "Win"], levels = c("Loss", "Win"), quiet = TRUE)
    tibble(
        Model         = model_name,
        Features      = n_feat,
        Test_AUC      = as.numeric(auc(rc)),
        Test_Accuracy = as.numeric(cm$overall["Accuracy"]) * 100,
        CV_AUC        = max(fit$results$ROC)
    )
}

grid_subsets <- list(
    Full        = colnames(X_train),
    Forward     = fwd_selected,
    LASSO       = lasso_selected$feature,
    ElasticNet  = enet_selected
)

grid_models <- c("LR", "NB", "KNN", "CART", "RF", "XGBoost")

grid_results <- map_dfr(names(grid_subsets), function(s) {
    map_dfr(grid_models, function(m) {
        fit_model_subset(m, grid_subsets[[s]]) %>% mutate(Subset = s)
    })
})

grid_results <- grid_results %>%
    mutate(
        Model  = factor(Model, levels = grid_models),
        Subset = factor(Subset, levels = names(grid_subsets))
    )

cat(sprintf(
    "Grid (%d cells) trained in %.1fs.\n",
    nrow(grid_results), as.numeric(Sys.time() - t0, units = "secs")
))

The total AUC range across the 24 cells is small relative to 5-fold CV noise, and most of it is CART under-performing the rest of the field rather than a selection-method effect. Across the four selection columns LR, KNN, RF, and XGBoost shift by at most 0.004 AUC, so for the strong learners feature reduction is essentially a parsimony decision rather than a performance one.

NB is the only model where reduction clearly helps, which is exactly what the S1 multicollinearity diagnosis predicted: dropping redundant predictors makes its likelihood factorisation closer to truth. Every other model is flat (LR, KNN, XGBoost) or marginally negative (RF, CART) - trees can use overlapping features at different splits, so reduction is mildly costly rather than helpful. The empirical answer to S1’s collinearity concern: feature selection here buys parsimony and interpretability, not higher held-out AUC.

13 Conclusions

13.1 H1 findings

H1 is confirmed. Every classifier trained on the 14 early-game features beats the 72.9% naive gold-rule baseline, and five of six exceed 83% AUC-ROC on the held-out test set. The test-set AUC values are 84.2% (LR), 83.0% (RF), 83.1% (NB), 83.7% (KNN), 79.7% (CART), and 83.8% (XGBoost). The spread between the top five is roughly 1 percentage point, meaning the feature set matters more than the model family - once you use a competent learner, the data determines the ceiling. CART trails the rest by ~3 pp, reflecting the limits of a single tree at this prediction ceiling.

Logistic Regression is the strongest single performer, edging out XGBoost and KNN by 0.4-0.5 pp AUC. This is the result a 14-feature pool with a clear linear signal should produce: when the dominant features (resource differentials at @15) carry a near-linear relationship with the log-odds of winning, a parametric linear model captures that signal as cleanly as a tree ensemble can. The cross-model feature importance consensus identifies golddiffat15, xpdiffat15, and csdiffat15 as universally important - the team that is ahead in gold, XP, and CS at 15 minutes wins with high probability. Binary objective flags (first dragon, first herald, first tower) add secondary, independent signal, but rank below the continuous resource metrics in importance.

These results sit in the published 76–78% accuracy band for 15-minute predictions on LoL professional data; our 83–85% AUC reflects the discriminative power of probability calibration over raw accuracy plus a broader feature set (14 vs. the 5–8 used in most prior work). Even in the 2025 season, where the reported predictive coefficient of golddiffat15 has declined, the early-game snapshot still yields a clear 10 pp AUC gain over the naive baseline.

13.2 H2 findings

H2 requires qualification. The EDA gives clear preliminary support: bot lane (ADC) has the highest Pearson correlation with match outcome among all five roles (r = 0.374), ahead of jungle (0.346), mid (0.338), support (0.316), and top (0.294). The inter-role gaps are narrow, so the full H2 test decides whether the bot lane edge is real or within noise.

The decisive test is the enriched Random Forest comparison after VIF cleanup: role-level granularity shifts RF AUC by only +0.5 pp over H1 (83.0% → 83.5%), inside the 5-fold CV noise band, so team-level totals already capture most of what the role split adds. The bot-lane ordering is the firmer half of the test: the EDA’s role-correlation chart gave bot lane the highest single-role correlation with blue_win, and the enriched RF ranks bot_golddiffat15 4th overall and first among per-role features - well above the best surviving feature of every other role. H2 therefore holds as an empirical ordering (bot lane leads), but not as a strong claim that bot lane alone drives prediction beyond team-level totals.

13.3 S1 vs S3 synthesis

S1 and S3 converge from two directions. S1 establishes that the 14 early-game features are collectively sufficient (83-84% AUC across five of six model families, CART trailing at 79.7%) with the signal concentrated in a compact core of continuous resource differentials at 15 min. S3 confirms and sharpens this: three independent selection methods - one algorithmic (forward stepwise by AIC) and two embedded (LASSO, Elastic Net) - all retain the same compact consensus core, while differing only in how aggressively they prune the marginal band beyond it.

The consensus set matches S1’s five-model importance consensus exactly: golddiffat15, xpdiffat15, csdiffat15, winrate_diff, firsttower, firstherald, firstdragon. The one disagreement of substance is kill_diff_15: it ranks reasonably high in unpenalised LR coefficients and tree-based importance scores, but pure LASSO (α = 1.0) zeroes it out as its signal is largely absorbed by golddiffat15 once L1 pressure is applied; Elastic Net (α = 0.90) keeps it. The downstream AUC difference between the two LR fits places the feature at the very margin of usefulness.

Recommendation: train on the consensus core. It is the subset on which all three independent criteria agree, and the validation grid shows that the AUC cost relative to the full 14-feature model is small enough to be inside CV noise. Features kept only by forward stepwise but dropped by both embedded methods - the marginal-contribution band identified in the S3 findings - sit below the L1 threshold and can be dropped without measurable loss. First blood is the clearest null result: despite its prominence in esports commentary, securing the first kill carries no independent predictive value once the 15-minute economic and objective picture is in.

dir.create("models", showWarnings = FALSE)

# Game lookup table for Shiny browser.
# The Shiny app's game-picker is per-side (one Blue and one Red row per game),
# so we un-pivot games_model back into a two-rows-per-game shape. Signed diffs
# are negated for the Red row, per-team kill counts are swapped, and binary
# flags are toggled (when Blue secured the objective, Red did not; otherwise
# we keep the same value, since neither team is recorded as having secured it).
shiny_blue <- games_model %>%
    mutate(side_encoded = 1L, result = blue_win) %>%
    select(-blue_win)

shiny_red <- games_model %>%
    transmute(
        gameid,
        side_encoded = 0L,
        result = 1L - blue_win,
        golddiffat15 = -golddiffat15,
        xpdiffat15 = -xpdiffat15,
        csdiffat15 = -csdiffat15,
        kill_diff_15 = -kill_diff_15,
        assist_diff_15 = -assist_diff_15,
        gold_efficiency_15 = NA_real_, # Blue-only ratio, no Red counterpart kept
        kda_15 = NA_real_,
        plate_diff = -plate_diff,
        grub_diff = -grub_diff,
        winrate_diff = -winrate_diff,
        firstblood = 1L - firstblood,
        firstdragon = 1L - firstdragon,
        firstherald = 1L - firstherald,
        firsttower = 1L - firsttower
    )

per_side_features <- bind_rows(shiny_blue, shiny_red)

# Per-side team labels
team_labels <- teams %>%
    select(gameid, league, date, side, teamname) %>%
    mutate(
        side_encoded = ifelse(side == "Blue", 1L, 0L),
        side_label = side
    ) %>%
    select(gameid, league, date, teamname, side_label, side_encoded)

opp_labels <- team_labels %>%
    transmute(gameid,
        side_encoded_opp = 1L - side_encoded,
        opp_teamname     = teamname
    )

game_lookup <- team_labels %>%
    left_join(opp_labels, by = c("gameid", "side_encoded" = "side_encoded_opp")) %>%
    inner_join(per_side_features, by = c("gameid", "side_encoded")) %>%
    mutate(
        date = as.Date(date),
        result_label = ifelse(result == 1, "WIN", "LOSS")
    )

saveRDS(game_lookup, "./models/game_lookup.rds")

# ROC objects for Shiny Model Comparison tab
roc_lr <- pROC::roc(y_test_fct, lr_prob[, "Win"], levels = c("Loss", "Win"), quiet = TRUE)
roc_rf <- pROC::roc(y_test_fct, rf_prob[, "Win"], levels = c("Loss", "Win"), quiet = TRUE)
roc_nb <- pROC::roc(y_test_fct, nb_prob[, "Win"], levels = c("Loss", "Win"), quiet = TRUE)
roc_knn <- pROC::roc(y_test_fct, knn_prob[, "Win"], levels = c("Loss", "Win"), quiet = TRUE)
roc_cart <- pROC::roc(y_test_fct, cart_prob[, "Win"], levels = c("Loss", "Win"), quiet = TRUE)
roc_xgb <- pROC::roc(y_test_fct, xgb_prob[, "Win"], levels = c("Loss", "Win"), quiet = TRUE)
saveRDS(
    list(lr = roc_lr, rf = roc_rf, nb = roc_nb, knn = roc_knn, cart = roc_cart, xgb = roc_xgb),
    "./models/roc_list.rds"
)
